articles.title: The Best Café in Town Turns People Away. Your System Should Too
articles.description: Two cafés, both completely full at 8:15 on a Monday. Both are about to turn away the next person...
articles.body_html:
Two cafés, both completely full at 8:15 on a Monday. Both are about to turn away the next person through the door. (Both imaginary. Probably.)

At the first café, you join the line. Nobody says anything. After four minutes you notice the barista has been looking straight through you since you walked in. Somewhere around minute five you work out that you are not getting a coffee.

At the second café, someone at the door says: "We're full for about ten minutes. The place next door has seats, and we'll be here when you're back."

Same capacity. Same number of people turned away. One café gets a thank-you and a regular. The other gets a one-star review and a story told at dinner.

Queue limits, load shedding and utilisation curves help decide when to say no. This post is about what the no itself looks like. In an API, the refusal is part of your interface. Client libraries, proxies, dashboards and a tired human at 3 a.m. all have to read it.

Five bad ways to say no

The Slow No. The server holds the connection for thirty seconds, tries everything, then gives up. The caller waited the whole time. A no that costs as much as a yes saves you nothing.

The Silent No. The connection just drops. Now the client has an impossible question: did the server start my request or not? Without an answer it can't know whether retrying is safe.

The Vague No. A 500 Internal Server Error with the body "Something went wrong." It's the barista saying "sorry, something happened" and going back to wiping the counter. A 500 signals an unexpected server-side condition. Busy is not necessarily broken, and callers deserve to know the difference.

The Lying No. A 200 OK with {"ok": false} in the body. Most HTTP-aware tooling treats a 2xx as success unless someone has configured it to look inside the body. Your status-based error metrics can sit at zero while customers go unserved. The dashboard stays very calm.

The Too-Late No. It takes the payment, then says sorry. Don't do anything irreversible, like charging a card, sending an email or committing a write, until the request has passed admission and your own validation. An admission refusal shouldn't start a payment or leave a write halfway through. Failures after admission need their own handling, including idempotency where appropriate.

What a good no is made of

  1. Early and cheap. Run the admission check as early as your framework allows, ideally before expensive body parsing, database work or downstream calls. The refusal should be the fastest thing your service does.
  2. The right status code. 429 Too Many Requests means this caller has sent too many requests in a given time. 503 Service Unavailable means the server can't handle the request right now, for example because it is overloaded. The client's next move is different in each case, so don't mix them up.
  3. A Retry-After that means something. RFC 9110 allows either a number of seconds or an HTTP date. It is a hint, not a promise, and it is optional. Base it on a real estimate of when you can accept requests again. If you can't make a useful estimate, leave it out instead of inventing one.
  4. A body a program can read. RFC 9457 defines "problem details": a small JSON object with optional members such as type, title, status and detail, served as application/problem+json. A client can branch on type instead of grepping a message.
  5. A promise about side effects. If the admission check runs before your work function, you can say so in your docs: a refusal from this layer means the work function never ran. That makes retries much simpler. Be precise about it, though. Authentication, logging or other middleware may already have run, and a gateway or load balancer in front of you can return its own 503 for reasons you don't control. Write down which refusals carry the promise.

Here is the server side, using only the standard library. work is an async function that does the real job:

import json
from collections import Counter

MAX_IN_FLIGHT = 8
in_flight = 0
refusals = Counter()


def refuse(status, reason, retry_after_seconds=None):
    refusals[reason] += 1
    body = {
        "type": "https://example.com/problems/at-capacity",  # use a URI you control
        "title": "Temporarily at capacity",
        "status": status,
        "detail": "Refused at the admission check, before the work function was called.",
    }
    headers = {"Content-Type": "application/problem+json"}
    if retry_after_seconds is not None:
        if type(retry_after_seconds) is not int or retry_after_seconds < 0:
            raise ValueError("retry_after_seconds must be a non-negative integer")
        headers["Retry-After"] = str(retry_after_seconds)  # a hint, not a promise
    return status, headers, json.dumps(body)


async def handle(request, work):
    global in_flight
    if in_flight >= MAX_IN_FLIGHT:
        # first thing handle() does: the work function hasn't been called
        return refuse(503, "server_busy", 2)
    in_flight += 1  # nothing awaits between the check and this line
    try:
        return 200, {}, await work(request)
    finally:
        in_flight -= 1

This is written for a single asyncio event loop, and the limit applies per process. The check and the increment can't be interleaved there, because nothing awaits between them. If you serve requests from several threads, or want one limit across several processes or machines, you need a different limiter. Treat the code as a teaching sketch, not a finished admission controller.

The 2 is a placeholder. Use a real estimate for your service, or pass nothing to leave the header out.

Taking a no well

A good customer takes a no well, too. That means reading the hint properly, waiting a little longer each time, adding some randomness so a crowd doesn't come back at the same second, and stopping eventually.

Retry-After comes in two forms, whole seconds or an HTTP date, so a client has to handle both:

import random
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime


def retry_after_seconds(value, now=None):
    if value is None:
        return None
    value = value.strip()
    if value.isascii() and value.isdigit():
        return float(value)
    try:
        when = parsedate_to_datetime(value)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return None
    if when.tzinfo is None:
        when = when.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    return max(0.0, (when - now).total_seconds())


def polite_retry(send, safe_to_repeat, max_tries=4, max_total_wait=30.0):
    if max_tries < 1:
        raise ValueError("max_tries must be at least 1")
    if max_total_wait < 0:
        raise ValueError("max_total_wait must be non-negative")
    deadline = time.monotonic() + max_total_wait
    delay = 0.5
    for attempt in range(1, max_tries + 1):
        status, headers, body = send()
        if status not in (429, 503) or not safe_to_repeat:
            return status, headers, body
        if attempt == max_tries:
            return status, headers, body  # hand the no back; don't swallow it
        hinted = retry_after_seconds(headers.get("Retry-After")) or 0.0
        wait = max(hinted, delay)
        wait += random.uniform(0, wait / 2)  # jitter
        if not wait <= deadline - time.monotonic():
            return status, headers, body  # out of budget: hand the no back
        time.sleep(wait)
        delay *= 2

This is a synchronous client, so it uses time.sleep; async code should use asyncio.sleep. It also assumes send() returns headers in a case-insensitive mapping, as requests and httpx do.

max_total_wait is a budget for the whole retry loop, and the time send() itself takes counts against it. If the next wait, or a Retry-After longer than what is left, would go past the budget, the client hands the no back instead of sleeping. The budget can't interrupt a send() that is already blocked, so give send() its own timeout.

safe_to_repeat is doing real work here. Reads, idempotent writes and calls carrying an idempotency key that the server actually enforces can be repeated. Ordering a coffee twice is not a retry. It's a bug with a receipt.

Count your nos

Every refusal should be counted, by reason. If refusals are handled quickly, their latency can stay low even as demand rises. The refusal count can be the graph that moves first when demand passes your limit. Keep watching latency for the requests you do accept, too, since a slow downstream can still stretch them. A no you don't count is a no you find out about from your customers.

It works on people, too

Everything above applies to the humans in your team. The Slow No is the request that sits in your inbox for three weeks. The Silent No is the unanswered message. The Vague No is "let's circle back." The Lying No is "sure!" followed by nothing. The Too-Late No arrives after the other person has built their plan on your yes.

A good no to a colleague has the same parts: early, quick, specific about what you're doing instead, honest about when they can ask again, and kind.

def can_you_just(ask):
    if ask["sounds_small"] and ask["touches_billing"]:
        # Not valid HTTP. Perfectly valid sprint planning.
        return 503, {"Retry-After": "next sprint"}
    return 200, {}

A yes you can't deliver is just a slow no.

What's the best no you've ever received, from a system or from a person?

articles.title: Introducing a Website That Absolutely Nobody Asked For
articles.description: I accidentally built a late-night television station for phishing websites.  Somewhere between...
articles.body_html:
I accidentally built a late-night television station for phishing websites.

Somewhere between collecting phishing screenshots, writing jokes about counterfeit login pages, and making fictional television commercials, I realized I was no longer building a cybersecurity dashboard.

I was building a television station for the worst parts of the internet.

Nobody asked for this.

I built it anyway.

It’s called Off-Brand.

The internet’s knockoff aisle.

⸻

The internet has some questionable merchandise

Spend enough time looking through public phishing records and you’ll eventually develop an appreciation for the sheer absurdity of what people put online.

Fake banks. Counterfeit cryptocurrency wallets. Delivery services operating out of suspicious domains. Corporate branding held together by questionable design decisions.

Some of these pages are surprisingly convincing. Others look like they were assembled during a lunch break.

But underneath the questionable craftsmanship is something worth studying: how these pages attempt to manufacture trust.

I wanted to explore that without creating another cybersecurity website that feels like mandatory employee training.

So naturally, I built a television station

Off-Brand is a screenshot comedy zine disguised as a late-night television broadcast.

Every specimen gets its own channel. You can flip between them, search the lineup, read the reviews, and occasionally get interrupted by a completely unnecessary commercial break.

There are channel-switching sounds, television static, scrolling captions, fictional advertisements, and a programming lineup.

Currently, the station has 30 published specimens and eight commercials, including:

  • Eau de Credentials — a luxury fragrance inspired by questionable decisions.
  • Support Your Local Knockoff Station — a public-access pledge drive for a station that nobody should financially support.
  • The Phishing Forecast — scattered login showers with a developing fake invoice front.
  • Somebody Stole Infinity — a museum security incident involving a suspiciously small infinity symbol.

The commercials are fictional productions, some created with generative media tools.

The specimens are not.

The entertainment can be fictional. The evidence cannot.

The joke is only half the product

As entertaining as it is to make fun of suspicious websites, I didn’t want Off-Brand to become a collection of superficial observations about bad web design.

A terrible-looking website isn’t necessarily malicious.

A beautifully designed website isn’t necessarily trustworthy.

Every published specimen includes a section called WHAT TO NOTICE, where the comedy gives way to technical observations and practical advice.

Take one of the USPS specimens, for example.

The captured page presents itself as a payment verification service. It claims a parcel is being held and requests a $1.95 redelivery fee.

The address?

uspsfund[.]online

USPS lives at usps[.]com. Putting USPS in another domain’s name doesn’t make that domain part of USPS. That’s somebody else’s mailbox.

According to the public scan record, the domain was observed on the day it was registered. The page requested cardholder information, card number, expiration date, CVV, and billing details.

View the public scan record for this specimen.

The small payment is part of what makes the request seem plausible. The information being requested is considerably more valuable than $1.95.

If you receive a message like this, visit the carrier’s official website directly rather than following the payment link.

That’s the kind of detail I want readers to notice.

Not just that a website looks suspicious, but why its behavior deserves scrutiny.

If someone visits for the ridiculous commercials and leaves knowing how to read a hostname correctly, I’ll consider that a worthwhile outcome.

Real specimens. Fictional programming.

The specimens are drawn from existing public records on urlscan.io.

I’m not deploying phishing pages, creating fake evidence, or sending visitors to malicious websites.

Suspect addresses are defanged, and every published review links to its public scan record.

Not every reported page deserves to be called phishing, either.

Some specimens remain explicitly unconfirmed. Others have been excluded from publication altogether.

Off-Brand even has a section documenting why certain specimens didn’t make the lineup.

The distinction matters. Making a good joke doesn’t make an unsupported accusation acceptable.

There are limitations, too. Public screenshots can disappear, third-party classifications are not infallible, and a historical scan doesn’t establish that a website is still active.

Off-Brand is a curated publication, not a real-time phishing detection service.

An unnecessarily serious amount of engineering

For something that looks like a television station with a questionable programming budget, Off-Brand has a surprisingly serious infrastructure underneath it.

  • Automated specimen collection with a private archive and explicit editorial approval.
  • Defensive handling of untrusted scan data and a restrictive Content Security Policy.
  • Fault-tolerant commercial playback, keyboard navigation, and reduced-motion support.
  • A suite of 122 regression checks required before deployment.

Even the commercial rotation has its own scheduling logic, playback safeguards, and recovery mechanisms.

Apparently, fictional television stations have infrastructure problems too.

The implementation and editorial standards are available in the public repository for anyone interested in looking under the hood.

Why bother?

I’ve spent a lot of time building security-related tools and writing about technical research.

Off-Brand gave me an opportunity to approach the subject differently.

Cybersecurity doesn’t always need another dashboard, another wall of statistics, or another article telling people not to click suspicious links.

Sometimes it might benefit from something people voluntarily explore because they’re curious about what happens when they change the channel.

I don’t know whether comedy makes phishing awareness more effective. I haven’t conducted a controlled study establishing that.

But it’s an interesting question.

And now I have a particularly strange platform for exploring it.

On the air

Off-Brand is free to explore, and its source code is publicly available.

  • Watch the broadcast: https://gnomeman4201.github.io/Off-Brand/
  • Inspect the source: https://github.com/GnomeMan4201/Off-Brand

I’d be interested in hearing whether the concept works for you.

articles.title: Your On-Device AI Works Offline. Does Your Web App?
articles.description: An on-device model can be ready without a network connection while the application around it still...
articles.body_html:
An on-device model can be ready without a network connection while the application around it still fails to reopen. The model works; the HTML, JavaScript, fonts, or saved input do not. From the user’s perspective, the feature is still offline and unavailable.

An offline promise therefore needs an interaction-level test. Close or reload the page without connectivity and check whether the person can recover their work, use the available features, and understand what is unavailable.

The companion implements a small React brief editor with local draft storage and a versioned application cache. Native AI remains optional and independently checked. The example does not queue bookings, synchronize accounts, or pretend that caching a shell turns a server-backed workflow into a complete offline application.

Track three independent kinds of readiness

The browser can have an application shell without a usable model, or a usable model without the application shell. The user’s draft is a third concern.

Resource Owner in this example Readiness question
HTML, JavaScript, CSS Application service worker Can the editor reopen?
Synthetic brief Application local storage Can the person recover the text?
Built-in AI model Browser Can the selected API perform this task?

Do not display a single “Offline ready” badge based only on successful service-worker registration. Registration does not establish that the worker controls this page, that all required assets were cached, or that the model can run.

Similarly, navigator.onLine is a connectivity hint. It cannot establish that a particular model endpoint or application API is reachable.

Cache the application shell deliberately

The build script collects the emitted HTML, JavaScript, and CSS and creates a cache name from their content hash. The generated service worker precaches that allowlist during installation.

self.addEventListener("install", event => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.open(CACHE).then(cache => cache.addAll(URLS))
  );
});

CACHE and URLS are build-generated values, not placeholders in the delivered worker. If installation cannot obtain a required asset, it should fail rather than advertise a complete shell.

The example handles the root navigation with a network request and a cached fallback. Versioned assets use the active shell cache. Requests outside the same-origin allowlist are left alone.

This restriction matters. A broad “cache every GET” policy can capture personalized responses, unbounded resources, and data whose freshness rules differ from static application code. The lab has no authenticated API responses to cache.

Treat updates as an application decision

A new worker cleans up older caches bearing this application’s prefix when it activates. It does not delete unrelated caches from the origin.

The example also avoids forcing every new worker to activate immediately with skipWaiting(). Replacing the worker beneath an open editor can mix versions or interrupt work. A larger application should offer a controlled update after the person has saved or exported their draft.

Keep old assets available on the server for a suitable deployment window. A versioned cache helps a previously installed application, but it cannot rescue an asset that was never cached and has already been removed from the server.

Figure 1. Offline editing and offline inference require different resources.

Preserve input without overstating storage

The demonstration stores a small synthetic brief in localStorage. Its write path catches failures and tells the person to copy the text before closing the page.

try {
  localStorage.setItem("web-ai-lab-brief", text);
} catch {
  setStorage("Local saving failed. Copy the brief before closing.");
}

This is intentionally modest. Storage is not a backup, a multi-device sync mechanism, or an appropriate default for every confidential document. Real products need a retention policy, deletion controls, and storage choices that fit their data and size requirements.

For a richer editor, IndexedDB may be more appropriate. Preserve the same user-facing rule: a failed write must not leave an unqualified “Saved” indicator on screen.

Keep model storage separate

The lab’s service worker does not attempt to cache Chrome’s built-in model internals. The application asks the API about the requested task and handles preparation or unavailability through the normal UI.

If you serve your own model through a library such as LiteRT.js, those model files and runtime assets become part of your application’s delivery design. Give them explicit versions, integrity records, download behavior, and cache rules. The companion excludes its benchmark’s model and Wasm files from the small editor-shell cache so that opening the editor does not silently download the benchmark workload.

Chrome’s model-caching guidance discusses models served by applications. Apply it to that delivery path rather than assuming every built-in model is a resource your service worker controls.

Test a cold visit and a returning visit separately

Build the production bundle with npm run build, then serve it with npm run preview. The development server deliberately does not register the production worker.

First load the application online, save a synthetic brief, and wait for the worker to become ready. Reload to establish control, then disable connectivity and reload again. Verify that the editor appears and that the saved text is correct.

Now repeat in a fresh profile that has never visited the application. An offline first visit has no installed shell to use. That should be reported as an unsupported scenario, not folded into a returning-user success rate.

The browser script passed this controlled-worker reload case in Headless Chrome 153. After saving a synthetic brief and establishing worker control, it disabled connectivity, reloaded, and recovered the exact saved text. The evidence file and screenshot record that result. This verifies the editor and draft; model inference still requires its own native preparation and offline run.

Finally test missing assets, storage failures, and a model that is unavailable even though the editor opens. A successful warm model call while the page remains open does not cover any of those scenarios.

The practical goal is continuity: people can recover their text and understand the remaining options. Which part of your application’s offline promise have you verified after a complete reload?

References

  • Service-worker caching strategies
  • Create an offline fallback page
  • Cache models in the browser
  • Chrome built-in AI APIs

articles.title: Next.js 16 use cache: remote vs use cache: private
articles.description: Next.js 16's use cache: remote shares a cache across instances; use cache: private never leaves one request. Which to pick, plus a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
A team ships personalized product recommendations on a product page. The data depends on the visitor's session cookie, so a teammate wraps the fetch in a plain 'use cache' function and reads cookies() inside it. next build passes. next start doesn't: every request to that route throws next-request-in-use-cache, because use cache cannot see request-time APIs at all, by design.

The fix looks obvious: switch to 'use cache: private', since the docs say it's the directive that can read cookies. It compiles, it renders, the recommendations are personalized again — and the team, having just learned there's a "private" cache, applies it everywhere else that used to be a plain fetch, including the currency-converted price that's genuinely the same for every visitor paying in USD. Three weeks later, the pricing API is getting hammered on every cold start in production, because 'use cache: private' was never meant to deduplicate shared data across users — it isn't that kind of cache at all.

This is the mix-up this article exists to prevent. Next.js 16 ships three caching directives under Cache Components — use cache, 'use cache: private', and 'use cache: remote' — and they answer three different questions, not one question three ways. This article is written against Next.js 16.4.6 (verified against the framework's own bundled documentation and npm's latest dist-tag in November 2026); both private and remote caches were introduced and stabilized together with Cache Components in Next.js 16.0.0.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain what each of the three use cache directives actually stores, and where
  • Pick the right one for personalized data, for shared-but-expensive data, and for everything else
  • Read the nesting rules that decide which directives can wrap which
  • Avoid the two opposite mistakes: caching personal data where it could leak, and caching shared data where it never gets reused

Who this is for

You're already caching something with plain 'use cache' — or you've read Next.js Cache Components Explained, which builds that foundation from nothing. This article assumes that part and goes one level deeper, into the two directives that exist specifically for data use cache can't handle. You don't need to have read it first; the rules below stand on their own.

Table of contents

  • The problem: one cache, three jobs it can't all do
  • The mental model: scope and storage are two different dials
  • Stage 1: the baseline — what plain use cache won't do
  • Stage 2: use cache: private — per-request, never shared
  • Stage 3: use cache: remote — shared across every instance
  • Stage 4: the nesting rules
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet

The problem: one cache, three jobs it can't all do

Plain use cache does two jobs at once: it tells Next.js what's safe to put in a route's prerendered static shell, and it caches a function's result so repeat calls with the same inputs skip the work. Both jobs assume the same thing — that the cached value is identical for every visitor who triggers the same inputs. That assumption breaks the moment a value depends on who's asking, which is exactly why use cache refuses to let you read cookies(), headers(), or searchParams inside it: there'd be no safe single value to put in a shell every visitor shares.

So the framework splits the "who's asking" problem into two separate directives, one for each half of it:

  • Sometimes the answer genuinely differs per visitor and must never be handed to anyone else — that's 'use cache: private'.
  • Sometimes the answer is the same for many visitors (same currency, same language, same product category) but you still need to defer reading it until request time, and the default in-memory cache isn't durable enough across your server instances — that's 'use cache: remote'.

Neither one is "the private version" or "the bigger version" of the other. They answer different questions, and reaching for the wrong one either leaks nothing useful (over-caching data that was never personal) or hammers your backend (under-caching data that should have been shared).

The mental model: scope and storage are two different dials

The mental model: every cache in Next.js is the product of two independent choices — who the cached value is allowed to be shared with (scope), and where it physically lives (storage). Conflating these two dials is the whole source of confusion here.

use cache 'use cache: remote' 'use cache: private'
Scope — who shares one entry Everyone Everyone Nobody but this one request
Storage — where it lives In-memory (or a configured handler) A remote cache handler (Redis, KV, …) Nowhere persistent — not saved across requests in production
Can read cookies() / headers() No No Yes

Read the table by column, not by row: use cache and 'use cache: remote' share the same scope (everyone) and differ only in storage durability. 'use cache: private' is the odd one out on scope — it exists purely to let request-specific code participate in caching at all, and the tradeoff for that access is that nothing it produces gets saved across requests.

Stage 1: the baseline — what plain use cache won't do

A quick recap, since both of today's directives are defined by contrast to this one. A plain cached function looks like this:

// app/lib/pricing.ts
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

export async function getBasePrice(productId: string) {
  'use cache';
  cacheLife('hours');
  return db.products.getPrice(productId);
}

This is shared across every visitor who asks for the same productId, and it can contribute to the route's static shell. The constraint: this function, and anything it calls, cannot touch cookies(), headers(), or searchParams — doing so throws next-request-in-use-cache the moment the route actually runs, even though next build may not have caught it.

Key concept: use cache isn't refusing to be "dynamic" out of caution — it genuinely has nowhere safe to put a per-visitor answer. That gap is exactly what the next two directives exist to fill, each for a different reason.

Stage 2: use cache: private — per-request, never shared

'use cache: private' lifts the ban on request-time APIs, at the cost of never sharing the result:

// app/product/[id]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<div>Loading recommendations...</div>}>
      <Recommendations productId={id} />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

async function Recommendations({ productId }: { productId: string }) {
  const sessionId = (await cookies()).get('session-id')?.value ?? 'guest';
  const recs = await getRecommendations(productId, sessionId);
  return <RecList items={recs} />;
}

async function getRecommendations(productId: string, sessionId: string) {
  'use cache: private';
  cacheTag(`recommendations-${productId}`);
  cacheLife({ stale: 60 });
  return db.recommendations.personalize(productId, sessionId);
}

In production, calling this function twice within the same request can reuse the result — that's request-scoped deduplication, not a server cache. It is never written to a cache that a later request, from the same visitor or anyone else, can read. In development, Next.js does keep it in memory, keyed by that request's cookies and headers, so you can watch it serve a near-identical dev request from cache — which is useful for iterating locally, but isn't the production behavior.

Key concept: the stale time you set with cacheLife governs the client-side router cache, not a server store. Private cache functions are excluded from static-shell generation entirely, so this value only controls how long the browser can reuse what it already streamed down. The docs call out a specific threshold: stale must be at least 30 seconds for per-link prefetching to work, and at least 5 minutes for the content to be eligible for the route's App Shell. If a function only needs within-request dedup and shouldn't shorten the route's overall client stale time, set cacheLife({ stale: Infinity }) — that opts it out of influencing the route's shortest stale time without claiming server persistence it was never going to get.

Stage 3: use cache: remote — shared across every instance

'use cache: remote' solves a completely different problem: use cache's default in-memory store is just that — in-memory, per instance. In a serverless deployment, each invocation can land on a different, short-lived instance, so the in-memory cache barely helps; every cold instance re-runs the work and re-hits your backend.

// app/product/[id]/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
import { cacheTag, cacheLife } from 'next/cache';

async function ProductPrice({ productId }: { productId: string }) {
  // Reading cookies defers this component to request time
  const currency = (await cookies()).get('currency')?.value ?? 'USD';
  const price = await getProductPrice(productId, currency);
  return <div>Price: {price} {currency}</div>;
}

async function getProductPrice(productId: string, currency: string) {
  'use cache: remote';
  cacheTag(`product-price-${productId}`);
  cacheLife({ expire: 3600 }); // 1 hour

  // Cached per (productId, currency) — a handful of currencies, not one entry per visitor
  return db.products.getPrice(productId, currency);
}

Notice what's 'use cache: remote', not 'use cache: private', in this example: the price depends on currency, which is read from a cookie, but currency is shared across potentially thousands of visitors. Caching it as "private" would create one cache miss per visitor for data that's identical across a whole currency; caching it as "remote" creates one shared entry per currency and lets every server instance hit that same entry.

A remote cache needs a real handler — Redis, a KV store, anything configured through cacheHandlers — which most hosting providers supply automatically, and which you configure yourself if you're self-hosting. That's the tradeoff 'use cache: remote' is explicit about: infrastructure cost and a network round trip on every lookup, in exchange for a cache that's actually shared once a request falls outside the static shell.

Key concept: reach for 'use cache: remote' only when the dimension you're caching on has few distinct values relative to your traffic (currencies, languages, categories — not user IDs or arbitrary search filters). The docs frame this as finding "the dimension with fewer unique values" and caching on that, then filtering the rest in memory. Cache on category, not on category + minPrice, and the hit rate difference is the entire point of paying for a remote handler at all.

Stage 4: the nesting rules

Because remote and private caches solve opposite problems, Next.js enforces where each can appear relative to the other:

  • A remote cache can nest inside another remote cache, or inside a plain use cache.
  • A remote cache cannot nest inside a private cache, in either direction. 
// VALID — remote inside a plain cache
async function outerCache() {
  'use cache';
  return innerRemote(); // fine — resolved when deferred to request time
}

// INVALID — remote inside private, or private inside remote, throws
async function outerPrivate() {
  'use cache: private';
  return innerRemote(); // Error
}

The rule follows directly from the mental model: a private cache's entire contract is "nothing here gets shared." Letting a shared remote cache live inside it (or vice versa) would mean one of the two guarantees has to break. Next.js enforces the rule at the boundary instead of leaving it to be discovered in production.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • Remote caches don't survive a deploy. The cache key for 'use cache: remote' includes your build ID (or deploymentId, if you've configured one), so a new build produces entirely new keys. This is intentional — a refactored function or an upgraded dependency can quietly change what a cache entry means, and reusing an old entry under a new build risks serving data that doesn't match what the new code expects.
  • Draft Mode bypasses use cache, no special case needed. The docs are explicit about plain use cache: with Draft Mode enabled, cached functions and components re-execute on every request and their results aren't saved to the cache. 'use cache: private' already never persists across requests in production, so Draft Mode doesn't change anything there either way. The docs don't make the same statement by name for 'use cache: remote' — don't assume it behaves identically without checking your own cache handler.
  • connection() is off-limits in both use cache and 'use cache: private'. It's easy to assume "private" means "anything request-related is now fair game," but connection() specifically carries connection-level information that isn't safe to cache even per-request, so it stays prohibited in both.
  • You can't configure a custom handler for 'use cache: private'. Unlike use cache and 'use cache: remote', there's no cacheHandlers hook for the private directive — by design, since it's defined by not persisting anywhere durable.
  • "Private" and "needs a database row per user" aren't the same problem. If what you actually need is data that survives across a user's many requests (not just within one), none of these three directives is the tool — that's your own data layer, read directly or behind a conventional cache.

Best practices

  • Default to plain use cache for anything that's genuinely identical for every visitor. It's the cheapest of the three — no extra infrastructure, and it's eligible for the static shell.
  • Reach for 'use cache: remote' only once you've confirmed the dimension you're caching on has low cardinality (a handful of currencies or categories, not one value per user) and the operation is slow or rate-limited enough to justify a network round trip to check.
  • Reach for 'use cache: private' only for data that's genuinely personal and either can't be refactored to read runtime values outside the cached scope, or has a real compliance reason it must never land in a shared store — the docs call this the narrow case, not the default.
  • Before adding any directive, ask whether the runtime value can simply be read outside the cached function and passed in as an argument. That's the preferred pattern for both use cache and 'use cache: remote', and it often removes the need for 'use cache: private' entirely.
  • Set an explicit cacheLife on every cache you write. The implicit default profile (5 minutes client-side stale, 15 minutes server-side revalidate) is a reasonable fallback, but it hides the lifetime at the call site — and for private caches specifically, forgetting it means forgetting to decide whether this function should shorten the whole route's client stale time.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Key takeaways

  • use cache, 'use cache: private', and 'use cache: remote' answer three different questions — shared/durable, personal/ephemeral, and shared/durable-but-deferred — not three strengths of the same cache.
  • 'use cache: private' lets you read cookies(), headers(), and searchParams inside a cached scope, but in production it never persists past the request that created it. It solves an access problem, not a sharing problem.
  • 'use cache: remote' solves the opposite problem: it shares a cache entry across every server instance, using a real handler, at the cost of infrastructure and network latency — and it only pays off when the cached dimension has few distinct values relative to your traffic.
  • Remote and private caches cannot nest inside each other in either direction, because their guarantees are mutually exclusive.
  • The cheapest fix for "I need runtime data in a cached function" is still reading it outside the cache and passing it as an argument — reach for private or remote only once that's genuinely not an option.

That team from the opening: the actual fix wasn't choosing between 'use cache: private' and 'use cache: remote' for the pricing function — it was recognizing that currency isn't personal data at all. The recommendations stayed on 'use cache: private', keyed per session, exactly as personal data should be. The price moved to 'use cache: remote', keyed on currency — a few dozen cache entries instead of one cache miss per visitor, and their pricing API went back to seeing the traffic it was built for.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

FAQ

Can I use 'use cache: remote' and 'use cache: private' together?

Not nested inside one another, in either direction — Next.js rejects that at the boundary. You can use both in the same route, on different functions, as the pricing-and-recommendations example above does; you just can't wrap one directive's scope inside the other's.

Does 'use cache: remote' persist across deployments?

No. Its cache key includes your build ID (or deploymentId if configured), so every new deploy invalidates every entry by construction. If you need data that survives a deploy, that's a job for unstable_cache (for non-fetch functions) or the fetch cache, not either of today's two directives.

Why doesn't my 'use cache: private' data show up for a different request?

Because that's the entire point of the directive. It isn't a bug or a cold-cache miss — 'use cache: private' is explicitly designed to never share its result across requests in production. If you need the same computed value available to a second request, you want use cache or 'use cache: remote' instead, with the request-specific part extracted and passed in as a plain argument.

How is 'use cache: remote' different from unstable_cache()?

Both can persist data outside the in-memory default, but they come from different eras of the same problem. unstable_cache() predates Cache Components, has its own key-building rules (notably, no awareness of root params), and the docs now point most use cases toward use cache and its Cache-Components-era siblings instead. If you're still using unstable_cache() for something that could be a cached function today, a cold-start cache-key leak between the two is worth reading about before you decide which one to keep.

Do I have to set up cacheHandlers myself to use 'use cache: remote'?

Usually not — most hosting providers wire up a default remote handler for you. You only need to configure cacheHandlers yourself if you're self-hosting and want remote caching, or if you want to swap in a specific store (Redis, a particular KV service) instead of whatever your platform provides by default.

What happens if I forget cacheLife on a private or remote cache?

The implicit default profile applies: 5 minutes stale (client-side), 15 minutes revalidate (server-side), and no time-based expire. It's a safe fallback, but for a private cache specifically, it also means you haven't deliberately decided whether this function should be allowed to shorten the whole route's client-side stale time — set it explicitly once you know the answer.

Cheat sheet 

NEXT.JS 16 CACHE DIRECTIVES — WHICH ONE?

                         use cache     use cache: remote   use cache: private
Shared across users?       yes              yes                  no
Can read cookies/headers?  no               no                   yes
Where it's stored          in-memory*       remote handler       nowhere durable
Survives a deploy?         no               no                   n/a
Needs cacheHandlers?       optional         yes (or platform)    not configurable
Contributes to static shell? yes            when static          never

* or a configured handler — see cacheHandlers

DECISION ORDER (ask in this order, stop at the first "yes"):
1. Can I read the runtime value OUTSIDE the cache and pass it in as an argument?
   → yes: use plain `use cache`. Done — you probably don't need private or remote.
2. Is the value genuinely personal / per-user, with no low-cardinality dimension
   to cache on instead?
   → yes: `use cache: private`. Set cacheLife({ stale: Infinity }) if it's pure
     within-request dedup and shouldn't shorten the route's client stale time.
3. Is the value shared across many users, deferred to request time, and worth
   paying infra + latency for a real cache hit (slow/rate-limited/expensive)?
   → yes: `use cache: remote`, keyed on the LOW-cardinality dimension
     (currency, locale, category) — never on something unique per request.
4. Otherwise: plain `use cache` with an explicit cacheLife.

NESTING
  remote  inside remote   -> OK
  remote  inside use cache -> OK
  remote  inside private   -> ERROR
  private inside remote    -> ERROR

next.config.ts (required for all three)
  export default {
    cacheComponents: true,
  }

articles.title: Recreating Vintage Cinema Ticket Effects in Pure CSS
articles.description: This year, I decided to participate regularly in the weekly CodePen challenges. My goal is simple:...
articles.body_html:
This year, I decided to participate regularly in the weekly CodePen challenges. My goal is simple: firstly, to keep my skills sharp, whilst exploring emerging web technologies; and secondly, to practise AI-augmented learning by utilising AI tools to examine technical topics from different angles.

Turning to this week’s challenge, the theme is "Experimental CSS". For this entry, I set out to explore and combine several modern CSS techniques, including corner-shape and scroll-driven timeline properties.

As this walkthrough covers quite a lot of ground, please feel free to brew yourself a cup of coffee and settle in for a detailed read.

Full disclosure: The initial concept and inspiration - vintage cinema tickets — were my own. From there, I experimented with a variety of AI tools and providers (I plan to cover the specifics of that workflow in a separate article). After several iterations, I arrived at a result I was pleased with, which I then refined and formatted into the final result you can see here.

Each iteration became noticeably faster using the following tools:

  • Claude Code
  • GPT-6.1 Terra and Mai Code 2 Flash via Github Copilot
  • Gemini Neon and modern web guidance via Antigravity

You can explore the completed demo in the CodePen below:

Why a ticket, and why pure CSS

A vintage cinema ticket is a small stress test for modern CSS: concave corners, punched half-moons, a ribbed texture, a hard offset shadow, a card that turns over, and a stack that fans open as you scroll. This article rebuilds all of it from a single combined file, with no JavaScript, no images, no SVG and no external fonts.

Pure CSS earns its keep here for three reasons. The effects stay in the cascade, so a ticket restyles with a custom property. Nothing blocks rendering, because there is no script to load. And every effect can sit behind @supports, so older browsers get a plainer ticket instead of a broken page.

The combined file merges the strongest parts of three drafts: a shared mask system, wrapper shadows, an @property fan, a film-strip progress bar, a :focus-within flip, clip-path stars and a two-layer hard shadow. All content is dummy test data ("Test Venue", "Sample Test Co.", 2099-01-01).

Setup: one wrapper, one ticket

Every ticket uses the same two-element pattern. The outer .ticket-wrap owns width and shadow. The inner .ticket owns paint, shape and masks. Splitting them matters: a mask clips everything inside an element, including its own shadow, so the shadow has to live one level up.

<div class="ticket-wrap">
  <article class="ticket t-coral" aria-label="Test voucher, admit one">
    <div class="stub"><p class="stub__admit">Admit One</p></div>
    <div class="chamber"><h3>Ticket</h3><p>Test Venue · No. 000001</p></div>
  </article>
</div>

.ticket-wrap { width: min(var(--w, 540px), 100%); }
.ticket-wrap--kraft { --w: 430px; }   /* set where it is read */

One bug from the earlier drafts is worth naming: --w was set on .ticket but read on .ticket-wrap. Custom properties inherit downward, never up, so the wrapper silently fell back to 540px. Set the width on the wrapper, or on a modifier class that sits on it.

Before: every ticket rendered at the default width. After: each ticket takes its own width and still shrinks on a phone.

Scooped corners with corner-shape

border-radius normally rounds a corner outward. corner-shape: scoop keeps the same radius but carves the corner inward, which is exactly the concave bite of a die-cut ticket. The radius still sets the size, so the two properties work as a pair.

.ticket {
  --r: 16px;
  border-radius: var(--r);          /* plain fallback, works everywhere */
}
@supports (corner-shape: scoop) {
  .ticket { corner-shape: scoop; }  /* only here */
}

The rule is strict: corner-shape appears only inside @supports (corner-shape: scoop). Outside it, the ticket keeps a normal border-radius, so layout never depends on the new property.

Browsers without support would show convex corners, which looks wrong for this design. So a second block, @supports not (corner-shape: scoop), adds four corner masks that reproduce the scoop:

@supports not (corner-shape: scoop) {
  .ticket {
    --corner-tl: radial-gradient(circle var(--r) at 0 0, #0000 94%, #000 100%);
    /* tr, bl, br follow the same pattern at 100% 0, 0 100%, 100% 100% */
  }
}

Before: rounded, soft-looking corners. After: concave bites in every browser, native where available and masked elsewhere. Note that the native path adds no masks for corners, so you never pay for both.

Perforations and cut-outs: intersected masks

Perforations are holes, and a mask is a stencil: opaque pixels stay, transparent ones vanish. Each hole is a radial-gradient that is transparent at the centre and opaque beyond its radius. Several stencils are stacked and combined with mask-composite: intersect, so a pixel survives only if every layer keeps it.

.ticket {
  --pr: 5px; --pitch: 22px;
  --perf-l: radial-gradient(circle var(--pr) at 0 50%, #0000 94%, #000 100%);
  --perf-r: radial-gradient(circle var(--pr) at 100% 50%, #0000 94%, #000 100%);
  --solid: linear-gradient(#000 0 0);
  --cut-a: var(--solid);  --cut-b: var(--solid);
  -webkit-mask-image: var(--perf-l), var(--perf-r), var(--cut-a), var(--cut-b);
  mask-image: var(--perf-l), var(--perf-r), var(--cut-a), var(--cut-b);
  -webkit-mask-size: 100% var(--pitch), 100% var(--pitch), 100% 100%, 100% 100%;
  mask-size: 100% var(--pitch), 100% var(--pitch), 100% 100%, 100% 100%;
  -webkit-mask-repeat: repeat-y, repeat-y, no-repeat, no-repeat;
  mask-repeat: repeat-y, repeat-y, no-repeat, no-repeat;
  -webkit-mask-composite: source-in;
  mask-composite: intersect;
}

The two side layers are tiles one --pitch tall, repeated down the edges, which gives the row of half-circle bites. The --cut-a and --cut-b slots default to a solid layer that changes nothing. A single ticket overrides them for its own cut-outs: the coral voucher punches half-moons at both ends of its dotted tear line, and the ribbed ticket notches its top edge.

Common mistake: forgetting the -webkit- pair. Older WebKit uses source-in where the standard says intersect; ship both.

Before: a plain rectangle. After: a stamped ticket whose holes are real transparency, so whatever sits behind the page shows through.

Shadows that follow the cut

A box-shadow draws a rectangle, ignoring masks and scooped corners. filter: drop-shadow() shadows the rendered pixels instead, so it hugs every notch. Because the mask lives on .ticket, the filter goes on the wrapper:

.ticket-wrap {
  filter: drop-shadow(0 14px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.38))
          drop-shadow(0 2px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.35));
}

Two soft layers, one wide and one tight, read as paper resting on a table.

The hard offset shadow. The terracotta banner swaps blur for a solid slab. Chained filters apply in order, so the second shadow wraps the first and creates a rim:

.ticket-wrap--hard {
  width: min(var(--w), calc(100% - 14px));
  margin: 0 14px 14px 0;   /* room for the offset */
  filter: drop-shadow(11px 11px 0 var(--hard))
          drop-shadow(13px 13px 0 var(--brass));
}

The margin is the detail people miss: a shadow offset past the box can overflow a narrow screen, so reserve its width.

Common mistakes: putting drop-shadow on the masked element, where it is clipped away, and giving the earlier draft's 4px value to a design described as 11px. Keep the spec text and the CSS in step.

Before: a rectangular shadow under a notched ticket. After: a shadow that carries every scoop and punched hole.

Texture and shapes with gradients and clip-path

Every surface is built from gradients, so there are no image requests.

  • Kraft grain: two repeating-radial-gradient layers at different pitches make speckle, a pair of soft radial blotches add stains, and box-shadow: inset 0 0 38px darkens the edges like aged card.
  • Fold crease: a narrow linear-gradient with a dark line and a pale highlight, angled at 260deg on the front and 95deg on the back.
  • Ribs: repeating-linear-gradient(90deg, ...) bands down both edges of the ribbed ticket.
  • Double frames: outline with a negative outline-offset draws a second hairline inside a border, with no extra element.

Stars come from clip-path, not glyphs, so they scale and recolour with ordinary CSS:

.stars i {
  display: block; width: 22px; aspect-ratio: 1; background: #ffd36b;
  clip-path: polygon(50% 6%, 62% 36%, 94% 38%, 69% 58%, 78% 92%,
                     50% 73%, 22% 92%, 31% 58%, 6% 38%, 38% 36%);
}
.chamber { border: 3px solid currentColor;
  outline: 1.5px solid rgb(255 242 223 / 0.6); outline-offset: -9px; }

Put the star polygon on a plain element and wrap the row in role="img" with an aria-label, so a screen reader hears "Five stars" once instead of five empty boxes.

Before: flat colour blocks. After: paper that looks handled.

A pure-CSS flip

The kraft ticket has a blank reverse. Turning it needs no script: a focusable container drives the rotation through :hover and :focus-within.

<div class="flip" tabindex="0" role="group" aria-label="Kraft ticket. Hover or focus to turn it over.">
  <div class="flip__inner">
    <div class="flip__face ticket-wrap"><article class="ticket t-kraft">…front…</article></div>
    <div class="flip__face flip__face--back ticket-wrap"><article class="ticket t-kraft"></article></div>
  </div>
</div>

.flip { perspective: 1200px; display: grid; }
.flip__inner { display: grid; transform-style: preserve-3d;
  transition: transform .8s cubic-bezier(.2,.7,.2,1); }
.flip__face { grid-area: 1 / 1; backface-visibility: hidden; }
.flip__face--back { transform: rotateY(180deg); }
.flip:hover .flip__inner,
.flip:focus-within .flip__inner { transform: rotateY(180deg); }

Both faces share one grid cell, so they stack without absolute positioning. Each face keeps its own wrapper, which means the drop-shadow stays on a flat element rather than being flattened out of the 3D context. tabindex="0" makes the card reachable by keyboard, and :focus-within turns it on tap for touch devices.

Common mistake: putting filter on the element that carries preserve-3d. A filter forces flattening and the back face stops hiding. Keep the filter on each face.

Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce the transition drops to 0.01ms, so the ticket still turns but without the animation.

Scroll-driven motion

Scroll-linked effects now run on the compositor timeline instead of scroll listeners. Three pieces do the work.

1. A film-strip progress bar. A fixed bar scales from 0 to 1 against the root scroller:

@keyframes film-advance { from { transform: scaleX(0); } to { transform: scaleX(1); } }
.film__fill { animation: film-advance linear both;
              animation-timeline: scroll(root block); }

2. Named view timelines. Each section declares a timeline, and timeline-scope on :root lets distant elements, such as the pill nav, use it:

:root { timeline-scope: --t1, --t2, --t3, --t4, --t5; }
#coral { view-timeline: --t1 block; }
.hud li:nth-child(1) a { animation-name: hud-pill; animation-timeline: --t1; }

Each pill lights up while its plate crosses the viewport, with no is-active class and no observer.

3. A registered property for the fan. A custom property cannot animate unless the browser knows its type. @property registers --fan as a number, so it interpolates from 0 to 1 and every ticket derives its own transform from it:

@property --fan { syntax: "<number>"; inherits: true; initial-value: 1; }
.deck__ticket { transform: translateX(calc(var(--tx) * var(--fan)))
                           rotate(calc(var(--rot) * var(--fan))); }
@keyframes fan-out { from { --fan: 0; } to { --fan: 1; } }
.deck__stage { animation: fan-out linear both; animation-timeline: --t5;
               animation-range: cover 28% cover 62%; }

One animated variable drives five rotations. The initial-value: 1 is the fallback: without scroll timelines the stack simply appears fanned.

All of this sits inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) and an @supports check, and the tall sticky deck only switches on there. Everywhere else the deck is a normal block.

Browser support and the @supports strategy

corner-shape is new and animation-timeline is still rolling out, so each feature gets a named fallback instead of a hope. Support changes quickly; check current compatibility tables before shipping.

Feature Where it lives If unsupported
corner-shape: scoop @supports (corner-shape: scoop) Four radial-gradient corner masks
mask-composite: intersect .ticket -webkit-mask-composite: source-in pair
animation-timeline @supports + reduced-motion media query Static page, dim full film strip
@property top of the stylesheet --fan: 1 set on :root, deck shows fanned

Three rules keep this honest:

  1. The new property appears only inside its own @supports block, never as a bare declaration.
  2. Every enhanced state has a sensible default state, so the page is complete before any enhancement applies.
  3. The fallback for corners is its own @supports not block, so a browser never runs both paths.

CSS-only feature flags. The hero shows which path the browser took, using no script. A pseudo-element holds the fallback text and @supports overrides it:

.flag--corner::before { content: "Mask fallback"; }
@supports (corner-shape: scoop) { .flag--corner::before { content: "Native scoop"; } }

That is a small, honest diagnostic: the label is true because the same condition that picked the shape picked the text.

Performance and accessibility

Performance.

  • Scroll timelines animate transform and opacity, which the compositor can handle without layout.
  • Masks and filter: drop-shadow repaint when their content changes. Keep filters on static wrappers and avoid animating a masked element's size.
  • Reveal animations on the whole .reveal wrapper are cheap; animating max-width in the HUD labels triggers layout, so keep that element small.
  • Gradients are generated, not downloaded, so the file has zero image requests.

Accessibility.

  • Each ticket is an <article> with an aria-label, and headings use real <h2> and <h3> elements.
  • Decorative parts (ribs, film strip) carry aria-hidden. The star row is one role="img".
  • Serial numbers sit in <data value="...">, so the machine-readable value travels with the text.
  • The flip works from the keyboard via tabindex="0" and shows a visible :focus-visible outline.
  • Colour tokens switch under prefers-color-scheme, and motion respects prefers-reduced-motion.
  • Watch contrast: tiny muted text on dark paper is the weakest spot. Keep captions at 0.8rem or larger and check them against the background.

Takeaways

  • Split shape from shadow: mask the inner element, filter the outer one.
  • Treat masks as stencils and combine them with mask-composite: intersect; leave default slots so one system serves every ticket.
  • Use border-radius plus corner-shape: scoop for the native corner, but only inside @supports, with a mask fallback in the matching @supports not block.
  • Register animated custom properties with @property so one variable can drive many transforms.
  • Give every enhancement a complete default, and let @supports and prefers-reduced-motion opt people in.
  • Put each custom property where it is read: a value set on a child never reaches its parent.

articles.title: You're debouncing search input. `useDeferredValue` skips the timer.
articles.description: A client-side filter over 10,000 rows doesn't need a server, so there's no network call to debounce — but the keystroke still stutters. useDeferredValue fixes the actual cause: a slow render, not a slow request.
articles.body_html:
Type react into a search box filtering 10,000 rows, and watch the input lag half a beat behind your own keystrokes. Open React DevTools and the component isn't broken — it's doing exactly what you told it to. It's just doing all of it, every time, before it lets the next character land.

The fix half the internet reaches for is a debounce. Wait 300ms after the user stops typing, then filter. It feels like it should work — fewer renders, less work. Try it in a real app and the stutter doesn't go away. It just moves to the end: the box stays suspiciously quiet for 300ms, then the final keystroke drags along a full re-filter of 10,000 rows, and that frame is the one that hitches.

Debounce was never fixing the slow part

Here's the part that's easy to miss: debounce doesn't make a render cheaper. It only makes it less frequent.

function Search({ items }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(query), 300);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);
  }, [query]);

  // still a synchronous, blocking filter — just a rarer one, thanks to
  // useMemo skipping it on the renders where `debounced` hasn't changed
  const results = useMemo(
    () => items.filter((i) => i.name.includes(debounced)),
    [items, debounced]
  );

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <List items={results} />
    </>
  );
}

debounced changes less often than query — that part works. But when it does change, filtering 10,000 rows and re-rendering however many of them matched still happens on the main thread, still blocking, in one synchronous commit. You've traded "stutters on every keystroke" for "freezes for one frame, 300ms after you stop." Neither one is "the input never lags" — and the freeze gets worse the more rows there are to render, not just the more rows there are to filter.

And there's a second cost nobody budgets for: that setTimeout is tracking state that has nothing to do with the server. If items is already in memory — no fetch, no endpoint, nothing to rate-limit — you've added a timer, a cleanup function, and a second piece of state to solve a problem debounce was never built for. Debounce exists to cut down how often a side effect fires. A local array filter isn't a side effect. It's a render.

Before you scroll — what's actually slow here: the filtering, or the fact that it runs on every keystroke?

The fix that doesn't ask you to pick a delay

useDeferredValue is a React hook built for exactly this split: let the input update immediately, every time, and let the expensive thing that depends on it lag behind on purpose.

import { useState, useDeferredValue, memo } from "react";

function Search({ items }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);
  const isStale = query !== deferredQuery;

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <div style={{ opacity: isStale ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
        <List items={items} query={deferredQuery} />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

// The filter has to live INSIDE the memoized component, keyed off the
// deferred value — that's what gives memo something stable to bail out on.
// Filtering in Search instead (and just handing List the result) would run
// the expensive work on every keystroke regardless of what's deferred.
const List = memo(function List({ items, query }) {
  const results = items.filter((i) => i.name.includes(query));
  return <ul>{results.map((i) => <li key={i.id}>{i.name}</li>)}</ul>;
});

No setTimeout. No "how many milliseconds feels right." query updates on every keystroke at full priority, so the input itself never lags — React treats typing as urgent and always renders it first. deferredQuery is a separate value that trails behind: React renders the list with the old deferred value first (cheap, since List is memoized and its props haven't changed), then — in the background, interruptible — renders it again with the new one.

That word, interruptible, is the actual mechanism, and it's the thing debounce can't do. If you type a second character before the deferred re-render finishes, React throws away that half-finished background work and starts over with the latest value, instead of finishing a now-stale render first. A debounce timer can't abandon work mid-flight like that — it can only decide when to start it.

Open your profiler and try both versions on a list of a few thousand rows. The debounced one shows long blocking tasks lined up end to end. The deferred one shows the same total filtering work, but broken into renders that each yield back to the browser — the keystroke you just made always wins the next frame.

Where it stops helping

useDeferredValue doesn't make filtering or rendering 10,000 rows faster. If that work takes 40ms, it still takes 40ms somewhere — the hook controls when React is allowed to start and finish that render relative to the next keystroke, and lets it move on to a newer update instead of committing a result that's already stale. If your list still needs virtualization or a better filtering algorithm, you still need to do that work; this just stops an already-reasonable render from fighting the keyboard for priority.

And it isn't a debounce replacement for the case debounce actually exists for: rate-limiting a request. If query drives a fetch to a search endpoint, you still want to wait before firing it — nobody wants an API call per keystroke, and useDeferredValue won't cut that count down, because it's a rendering primitive, not a networking one. Keep debouncing the request. Stop debouncing the render.

The isStale flag is worth keeping even once the lag is gone — not for performance, but for honesty with the reader: a slightly dimmed list for the few milliseconds between "you typed" and "the filtered results landed" tells them the app noticed their keystroke, instead of silently pretending nothing happened.

Next time a search box or a filter panel stutters, check which one you actually have: a request worth delaying, or a render that was never doing it concurrently in the first place.

The part worth keeping

Debounce answers "how often." useDeferredValue answers "what's allowed to interrupt what." They look like the same fix because they both make a laggy search box feel better — but only one of them is actually about rendering, and a search box filtering data you already have is a rendering problem first.

articles.title: CSS Transitions Skip display: none. transition-behavior Fixes That.
articles.description: You can finally animate a dialog in from display: none without JavaScript — transition-behavior and @starting-style turn the jump-cut into a real transition.
articles.body_html:
You build a dialog. You add transition: opacity 0.2s, transform 0.2s. You open it.

It just appears. No fade, no slide — a jump-cut, like someone spliced the film.

You check the transition is spelled right. It is. You check the element is actually changing opacity. It is — from 0 to 1, exactly like you wrote it. So why does it still snap?

Because the element isn't only changing opacity. It's also going from display: none to display: block, and CSS has never known how to transition that.

The property transitions can't touch

display isn't a number, a color, or a length. You can interpolate opacity: 0 to opacity: 1 because the browser can compute every value in between — 0.3, 0.7, whatever the easing curve wants at that frame. There is no value "in between" none and block. An element is either laid out or it isn't.

Properties like this are discrete: display, content-visibility, overlay, visibility (sort of — more on that below). The browser's only option has always been to flip them the instant the transition starts, which for display means none → block happens at frame zero, before your opacity transition even gets going.

So the classic workaround was: don't touch display at all.

.modal {
  opacity: 0;
  visibility: hidden;
  transition: opacity 0.2s, visibility 0.2s;
}
.modal.open {
  opacity: 1;
  visibility: visible;
}

visibility gets special-cased by the spec — browsers flip it to visible at the start of the duration when opening, and to hidden at the end when closing, so it doesn't clip the fade. It works, and it's not even an accessibility bug: visibility: hidden does pull the element out of the accessibility tree and the tab order while it's hidden. The real downside is layout — visibility: hidden never collapses the box, so the element still occupies its space the whole time, leaving a gap or pushing siblings around until you cover it with something else. The actual fix, for years, meant display: none toggled from JavaScript on a transitionend listener, timed by hand, one more thing to get wrong.

Guess which part people got wrong most. If you said "the timeout that doesn't match the CSS duration," you've shipped this bug too.

What changed

transition-behavior: allow-discrete tells the browser: include this property in the transition anyway. Instead of flipping at frame zero, a discrete property now flips at the very end of the transition when going from a value to none-equivalent, or at the very start when going the other way — same rule visibility already followed, just available to properties that never had it.

.modal {
  display: none;
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 0.2s, display 0.2s allow-discrete;
}
.modal.open {
  display: block;
  opacity: 1;
}

Try that alone, though, and you'll hit the next wall. The modal now fades out correctly — display stays block for the full duration while opacity eases to 0, then flips to none. But fading in still snaps, because on the very first frame the element goes straight to display: block; opacity: 1. There's no "starting point" to ease from — the element didn't exist in a transitionable state a moment ago.

That's what @starting-style is for.

.modal {
  display: none;
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 0.2s, display 0.2s allow-discrete;

  @starting-style {
    opacity: 0;
  }
}
.modal.open {
  display: block;
  opacity: 1;
}

@starting-style defines the values the browser should treat as "the frame before this element entered the DOM or became displayable." Without it, there's nothing before frame zero to transition from — the browser has no prior value, so it has nothing to interpolate. With it, the moment display flips to block, the element starts at the @starting-style values and transitions toward its real ones.

Three pieces, each covering a gap the others leave:

  • allow-discrete lets display itself sit in the transition queue instead of jumping
  • @starting-style gives the element an entry state to animate from
  • your normal transition and target values do the actual easing, same as always

Drop any one and you're back to a jump-cut on either the way in, the way out, or both.

Try it before you believe it

Toggle the panel below with and without allow-discrete wired up. Same markup, same duration — the only difference is whether display is allowed into the transition.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that still trips people up

content-visibility: hidden and the native <dialog>/popover overlay property are discrete too, and they're exactly where this combination earns its keep — you get the rendering-skip benefits of content-visibility and an entrance animation, which used to be mutually exclusive. If you're already using content-visibility: auto to skip offscreen rendering, allow-discrete is how you animate the same element's reveal without giving that performance win back.

One honest caveat: this is about transition, not animation. Keyframe animations have had @starting-style-adjacent control for longer via animation-fill-mode, and discrete properties behave a little differently inside @keyframes than inside a plain transition. If your modal uses animation instead of transition, check the specific property's behavior before assuming allow-discrete is even the piece you're missing.

And it's not magic for every discrete property — transition-behavior: allow-discrete only changes when the flip happens relative to the transition's duration. It still can't interpolate display: block to display: flex, because those aren't "on vs off," they're two different values with no path between them. The trick only works for the none ↔ something-else case.

Support is more uneven than it looks. Chrome 117 shipped the full combination — including animating display itself — soon after transition-behavior landed. Safari took two steps: 17.4 added transition-behavior and parsed allow-discrete, but didn't extend the discrete-property flip to display until Safari 18. Firefox shipped transition-behavior and @starting-style in 129, but as of late 2026 it still doesn't reliably transition display itself — closing transitions in particular can cancel and jump straight to none instead of running the full duration, a long-standing, still-open limitation rather than a recent regression. So build for the gap: the worst case should be the old jump-cut, not broken layout, but on today's Firefox that jump-cut can still show up on close.

Test what you actually know

That jump-cut modal isn't a display bug you work around anymore — it's three CSS features doing exactly what they say: allow-discrete admits the property into the transition, @starting-style gives it a place to start from, and your existing transition line does the rest.

Next time you reach for a setTimeout to delay a display: none, try deleting it instead. What's the last place in your codebase where JavaScript is still faking something CSS can now do natively? I'd genuinely like to know — drop it in the comments.
