articles.title: Template Literal Types Explained: Catching Path Typos at Compile Time
articles.description: A typo'd dot-path like "theme.colros.primary" compiles clean and fails silently at runtime — template literal types make TypeScript catch it before you ship.
articles.body_html:
Somewhere in your codebase there's a function that looks like this:

function get(obj: any, path: string) {
  return path.split(".").reduce((acc, key) => acc?.[key], obj);
}

const primaryColor = get(config, "theme.colros.primary");

Read that path again. colros, not colors. TypeScript compiles it without a single complaint. The app ships. primaryColor is undefined, some fallback kicks in, and the button is the wrong shade of blue for three weeks before a designer notices and files a ticket nobody can reproduce on the first try.

The type system had everything it needed to catch this. config has a real, known shape. The bug is a four-character typo in a string literal sitting right there in the call site. And TypeScript let it through anyway — because as far as the compiler is concerned, path: string accepts literally any string.

Here's the part that's easy to miss: fixing this isn't a runtime check. It's a type you can write yourself, today, in about fifteen lines, using a feature TypeScript has shipped since 4.1.

Why path: string can't save you

The naive get function above type-checks because string is the type. Every string is a string. TypeScript has no way to know that "theme.colros.primary" isn't a real path on config unless something narrower than string is doing the asking.

You could reach for keyof to type a single level:

function getTop<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}

That's genuinely safe — getTop(config, "theem") is a compile error. But it only goes one property deep. The moment you want "theme.colors.primary", you're back to a plain string, because keyof T gives you "theme", not "theme.colors.primary".

What you actually want is a type that looks at T and produces the union of every valid dot-path through it — and that's exactly what template literal types, combined with recursive conditional types, build.

Building the path type

Template literal types let you glue string literal types together the way you'd glue strings with ${} in a template string, except it happens at the type level:

type Greeting = `Hello, ${string}`;
// matches "Hello, world", "Hello, ", but not "Hi there"

That's the primitive. The trick is combining it with a mapped type over keyof T that recurses into each property:

type Primitive = string | number | boolean | bigint | symbol | undefined | null | Date;

type Paths<T> = T extends Primitive
  ? never
  : T extends readonly unknown[]
    ? never
    : {
        [K in keyof T & string]: T[K] extends Primitive
          ? K
          : K | `${K}.${Paths<T[K]>}`;
      }[keyof T & string];

Read it as: for every key K on T, if the value at that key is a primitive, the path stops there — just K. If it's an object, the path is either K itself or K followed by a dot and a valid path through that nested object. The [keyof T & string] at the end collapses the mapped type into a plain union.

Give it this Config:

interface Config {
  theme: {
    colors: { primary: string; secondary: string };
    darkMode: boolean;
  };
  name: string;
}

Paths<Config> resolves to:

"name" | "theme" | "theme.colors" | "theme.darkMode" | "theme.colors.primary" | "theme.colors.secondary"

Every single one of those strings is a real path on a real Config. There's no way to spell a typo and have it type-check, because the union was generated from the object's own declared shape, not typed by hand.

Making get use it

The path type alone doesn't fix get — you still need the return type to follow the path, or every call collapses to unknown. That's a second recursive conditional type, walking the string apart instead of the object:

type PathValue<T, P extends string> = P extends `${infer Head}.${infer Rest}`
  ? Head extends keyof T
    ? PathValue<T[Head], Rest>
    : never
  : P extends keyof T
    ? T[P]
    : never;

function get<T, P extends Paths<T>>(obj: T, path: P): PathValue<T, P> {
  const parts = (path as string).split(".");
  let current: unknown = obj;
  for (const part of parts) current = (current as Record<string, unknown>)?.[part];
  return current as PathValue<T, P>;
}

PathValue pattern-matches the string literal P against `${infer Head}.${infer Rest}`. If there's a dot, it peels off the first segment and recurses on the rest; once there's no dot left, it looks the final segment up with T[P] directly.

Now run the typo through it:

get(config, "theme.colors.primary"); // string — correct, and TypeScript knows it
get(config, "theme.colros.primary"); // compile error, not a runtime surprise

That second line doesn't run. It doesn't ship. tsc stops it with:

Argument of type '"theme.colros.primary"' is not assignable to parameter of type
'"name" | "theme.colors.primary" | "theme" | "theme.colors" | "theme.darkMode" | "theme.colors.secondary"'.

I ran both versions through tsc --strict before writing this — the naive one takes the typo silently, the typed one refuses to compile it. That's the entire payoff: the same information that used to surface as a confused designer three weeks later now surfaces as a red squiggle while you're still typing the call.

If you've ever typed a field name into react-hook-form's register("user.address.city") and had autocomplete walk you through it, you've already used a type built this same way — their Path<T> helper exists to solve exactly this problem for form fields.

Where this gets expensive

Two honest limits, because a type that silently falls back to any on hard cases is worse than no type at all.

Depth. TypeScript caps how deeply it will recurse into a conditional type. For most app config, form, or API-response shapes — three or four levels of nesting — Paths<T> resolves fast and correctly. Push it at a genuinely deep, non-recursive chain (I tested around sixty levels) and you'll hit Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite. At that point the fix is a depth-limited variant (cap the recursion with a counter type), not pushing harder on the same approach.

A type that references itself behaves differently, and worse. Give Paths an interface TreeNode { value: string; children: TreeNode } and TypeScript refuses outright with a different error — Type of property 'children' circularly references itself in mapped type — because the mapped type can't even start resolving a property whose type is itself. But the shape real trees actually use, children: TreeNode[], doesn't error at all: Paths<T> already bails out on arrays, so Paths<TreeNode> quietly resolves to just "value" | "children" — technically correct, but silently blind to everything nested under children. That's the failure mode worth losing sleep over: not a loud compiler error, but a type that compiles clean and just stops short of where you assumed it reached.

Arrays. The Paths<T> above explicitly bails on arrays (T extends readonly unknown[] ? never) rather than pretending to support them. Indexing into arrays by position (items.0.name) is a real, solvable extension — using `${number}` as a key — but it's a deliberately separate problem from object paths, and bolting it on half-finished is how you end up with a type that compiles but lies.

Neither of these is a reason to skip the type. They're the reason to know, before you reach for it on a 12-level GraphQL response, that you're past where it comfortably lives.

🎮 Try it yourself

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The next time you write obj[a][b][c] with a string you typed from memory, ask yourself whether TypeScript actually checked it — or just trusted you. What's the last path typo that made it past your compiler and into production? I'd genuinely like to know I'm not the only one.

articles.title: `use()` Breaks the Rules of Hooks on Purpose. Here's the Catch.
articles.description: React's `use()` reads a promise or context mid-render and skips the Rules of Hooks on purpose — but that same freedom hides a caching trap that resuspends your component forever if you miss it.
articles.body_html:
You rip out a useEffect, a useState, and a cleanup flag, replace all three with one line of use(), and the component looks cleaner than it has in months. Then you refresh the page and the loading spinner never stops. Network tab: the same request, firing again, and again, every few milliseconds, forever.

Nothing in the code is wrong, exactly. You just found the one rule use() actually enforces — by being the React API that's allowed to break every other rule.

The dance use() was built to end

Before use(), reading an async value inside a component meant writing the same fifteen lines everywhere:

function Profile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(() => {
    let cancelled = false;
    setLoading(true);
    fetchUser(userId).then((data) => {
      if (!cancelled) {
        setUser(data);
        setLoading(false);
      }
    });
    return () => { cancelled = true; };
  }, [userId]);

  if (loading) return <Spinner />;
  return <UserCard user={user} />;
}

Two pieces of state tracking one value. A cancelled flag so a slow response for the old userId doesn't overwrite a faster one for the new userId. None of it is about showing a user card — it's all plumbing to make useEffect behave like something it was never built to be: a way to read an async value.

use() reads it directly. No useEffect, no useState, no race-condition flag:

import { use, Suspense, useMemo } from "react";

function Profile({ userPromise }) {
  const user = use(userPromise);
  return <UserCard user={user} />;
}

function ProfilePage({ userId }) {
  const userPromise = useMemo(() => fetchUser(userId), [userId]);
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
      <Profile userPromise={userPromise} />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

use(userPromise) either returns the resolved value or, if the promise is still pending, suspends — the same mechanism React.lazy uses. React walks up to the nearest <Suspense> and shows its fallback instead of rendering Profile with nothing. When the promise settles, React re-renders Profile, and use() just returns the value like it was there all along. One line replaced the whole dance, and the race-condition flag is gone because there's only one state to track: the promise.

Before you scroll — does anything in that second version look like it could go wrong? Sit with it for a second.

I simplified it one line further. That's when it broke.

The useMemo felt like an extra step, so I cut it:

// 🚫 looks identical, isn't
function Profile({ userId }) {
  const user = use(fetchUser(userId));
  return <UserCard user={user} />;
}

This is the version that floods the network tab. Here's why: every time Profile renders, fetchUser(userId) runs again and hands use() a brand-new promise object — even if userId hasn't changed. React has no way to know that this new promise represents "the same request, still loading." It only knows it was just handed a pending promise it's never seen before, so it suspends again. The fallback shows, the promise eventually resolves, Profile re-renders, and on that render it calls fetchUser(userId) one more time — producing yet another new, unseen, pending promise. The loop doesn't stop because nothing ever breaks the chain.

useMemo was never decoration. It was the one thing making the promise's identity stable across renders — the same promise object came back out every time, as long as userId stayed the same — so React could recognize "I've already seen this one, it's done, here's the value" instead of "new pending work, suspend again."

That's the actual rule use() enforces, and it's stricter than anything useEffect ever asked of you: the promise has to come from somewhere that caches it. That's usually one of three places — a parent component that memoizes it (like the useMemo above), a Server Component, where the promise can be created fresh each request because the request itself is the cache boundary, or a Suspense-integrated data library (React Query, SWR, Relay) that's already solving this for you. Creating a fresh promise inside the same component that calls use() on it, every render, is the one pattern that's never safe.

One thing worth knowing before you lean on the useMemo version in production: React's own docs skip useMemo for this and reach straight for a persistent cache (a module-level Map keyed by the request, so the same promise comes back no matter what re-renders) — because useMemo is documented as a performance optimization, not a guaranteed one. It works in the ProfilePage/Profile split above specifically because the memo lives in the parent, and the parent never suspends. Move that same useMemo down into the component that calls use(), and the first suspend throws the memoized value away with it — recreating the exact loop you were trying to fix.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Why it's an API, not a hook

Here's the part that's easy to miss if you only skim the React docs: use() doesn't sit on the "Hooks" page with useState and useEffect. It's listed separately, under React's general APIs — and that placement isn't an accident of alphabetizing.

Every other hook comes with the Rules of Hooks: call it unconditionally, at the top level, in the same order, every render. Break that rule with useState and React's internal bookkeeping desyncs — state attaches to the wrong slot. use() doesn't have that problem, because it isn't tied to a slot in the same way. You can call it inside an if, after an early return, or inside a loop:

function Message({ isLoggedIn, messagePromise }) {
  if (!isLoggedIn) {
    return <LoginPrompt />;
  }

  // Calling use() AFTER an early return is exactly what useState forbids.
  const message = use(messagePromise);
  return <p>{message}</p>;
}

A real hook here would be a lint error. use() is fine with it, because React re-evaluates each call to use() on its own, by reading from the thing you passed it, not from a fixed position in a call sequence. The same freedom applies to use(SomeContext) — unlike useContext, you can read it conditionally, which is genuinely useful for a component that only cares about a context value in one branch.

The freedom has a boundary, though: you can't wrap use() in your own try/catch. If the promise rejects, use() throws, and React expects an Error Boundary above it to catch that throw — the same contract as a render that throws for any other reason. If you want to handle the rejection yourself instead, attach .catch() to the promise before handing it to use(), so it never actually rejects on React's end.

The part worth keeping

use() isn't "useEffect but shorter." It's a different contract: you hand it something that eventually has a value, and it pauses the render until that value exists — but only if what you hand it stays recognizably the same thing across renders. Skip the caching and you get the one failure mode worse than the useEffect dance you were trying to delete: a spinner that looks broken but is actually working exactly as told, forever.

Where in your own code is a promise getting created fresh on every render because moving it up one level felt like overkill? That's the one to check first — before use() finds it for you in production.

articles.title: Your WebSocket Reconnects Fine. The Messages It Missed Never Do.
articles.description: Exponential backoff fixes the reconnect storm. It does nothing for the messages your server sent while the socket was down — those need an app-level replay, or they're gone for good.
articles.body_html:
The badge in the corner goes from green to red to green again. Three seconds, tops — long enough to walk through a subway turnstile, short enough that nobody files a bug. Your reconnect logic did exactly its job: it noticed the drop, waited, and opened a fresh connection before the user even looked up.

Two days later, someone on your team says "wait, I never got the update you pushed at 2:14." You check the logs. The server sent it. The client was definitely connected by 2:16. The message is just gone.

It's gone because "reconnected" and "caught up" are two different claims, and the reconnect loop only ever promised the first one.

The reconnect code almost everyone writes first

Here's the version that looks obviously correct:

function connect(url) {
  const ws = new WebSocket(url);
  ws.onmessage = handleMessage;
  ws.onclose = () => connect(url); // reconnect — done, right?
  return ws;
}

Run it against a flaky connection and it works. The socket drops, onclose fires, a new WebSocket opens, messages flow again. Watch the status indicator and you'll see exactly what you wanted: disconnect, brief gap, reconnect.

The test that never runs is the one where the server is the one that went away — a deploy, a restart, a load balancer hiccup that drops every open connection at once. Now every client's onclose fires within the same few hundred milliseconds, and every one of them calls connect() immediately. The server comes back up to a wall of simultaneous reconnection attempts from everyone it was serving a second ago — the same retry-storm problem that shows up in any naive retry loop, just wearing a WebSocket instead of a fetch().

Backoff and jitter fix the storm

The fix is the same one that works for HTTP retries: wait, and don't all wait the same amount.

function createReconnectingSocket(url, onMessage, { baseDelay = 500, maxDelay = 15000 } = {}) {
  let ws, attempt = 0, closedByClient = false;

  function connect() {
    ws = new WebSocket(url);
    ws.onmessage = onMessage;
    ws.onopen = () => { attempt = 0; };
    ws.onclose = (event) => {
      if (closedByClient || event.code === 1000) return; // a deliberate, clean close — don't reconnect
      const windowMs = Math.min(maxDelay, baseDelay * 2 ** attempt);
      attempt++;
      setTimeout(connect, Math.random() * windowMs); // full jitter — spread attempts, don't synchronize them
    };
  }

  connect();
  return { close: () => { closedByClient = true; ws.close(1000, "client closed"); } };
}

Two details carry the fix:

  • event.code === 1000 is a clean, intentional close — the server said goodbye on purpose, or you called .close() yourself. Reconnecting after that would fight your own shutdown logic. Everything else — including 1006, the code the browser assigns when the connection just vanishes with no close frame at all — is the "something broke, try again" case.
  • Math.random() * windowMs is full jitter: instead of every client waiting exactly 500ms, then exactly 1000ms, then exactly 2000ms (which just re-synchronizes everyone into new, smaller storms), each client picks a random point inside the growing window. The server sees a trickle of reconnects instead of a wave.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Watch six simulated clients reconnect after a shared outage, with and without jitter, and the storm either does or doesn't happen in front of you.

Ship that, watch the status line go disconnected → reconnecting → connected smoothly, and it's tempting to call this done. The UI agrees with you. That's exactly the problem.

Reconnecting is not resuming

A WebSocket has no concept of "pick up where we left off." When connect() runs again, it isn't un-pausing the old socket — it's opening a completely new one, with its own handshake, that the server has never seen before. There is no frame in the spec for "resend me everything since sequence 41." If your server tried to send() a message to a socket that was already closed, that call either no-ops or throws — either way, the message isn't queued anywhere waiting for you to come back.

So picture the actual timeline from the hook above: connection drops at 2:14:02, your server pushes an update at 2:14:05 to a socket that no longer exists on the other end, your client reconnects at 2:14:06. The new connection is healthy. The update from 2:14:05 was never sent to this socket, because this socket didn't exist yet when it was sent. Nothing errored. Nothing logged a failure. The badge is green. The data just isn't there.

This is the gap every "add exponential backoff and you're done" tutorial skips, because backoff genuinely does solve the problem it's aimed at — the storm. It was never aimed at message loss, and a smooth-looking reconnect makes that easy to forget.

The actual fix: let the client ask what it missed

Recovering the gap needs a contract the WebSocket protocol doesn't give you for free — so you build a small one on top of it. The shape is always the same three pieces:

  1. Every message the server pushes carries an increasing sequence number.
  2. The client remembers the last one it successfully processed.
  3. On reconnect, the client asks for everything after that number, before it trusts the new connection as caught up. 
let lastSeq = 0;

function handleMessage(event) {
  const msg = JSON.parse(event.data);
  if (msg.type === "resume-complete") return; // see below
  lastSeq = Math.max(lastSeq, msg.seq);
  render(msg);
}

function onSocketOpen(ws) {
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "resume", since: lastSeq }));
}

The server's half of the deal is the part that actually matters: it needs to keep a short rolling buffer per connection (or per user) of recently sent messages, so a resume request can be answered by replaying the ones after since. That buffer can't be infinite — if a client comes back after being offline for an hour and the server only kept five minutes of history, the honest answer is not to silently pretend nothing was missed. It's to tell the client its since is too old and trigger a full resync (a normal REST fetch of current state), the same way a CDN tells you a cache entry expired instead of serving stale data as if it were fresh.

That buffer-and-replay logic lives on the server and is genuinely more work than the client-side backoff loop. It's also the only part of this that actually answers "did I get everything," which is the question the green badge was never answering in the first place.

One more thing backoff doesn't catch: the socket that's dead but doesn't know it

There's a second failure mode worth closing out, because it breaks the resume logic above in a sneaky way: a laptop goes to sleep, or a phone's network stack silently drops a connection without telling the browser. ws.readyState can report OPEN for a socket that network hardware gave up on minutes ago — no close event fires, so none of the reconnect logic above ever triggers, because as far as your JavaScript knows, nothing happened.

The browser's WebSocket object gives you no way to send a protocol-level ping to check — there's no .ping() method in the standard; that exists on server-side libraries like Node's ws package, not in the browser API. So you build the check into the one channel you do control: your own messages.

function startHeartbeat(ws, { interval = 20000, timeout = 5000 } = {}) {
  let pongTimer;
  const pingTimer = setInterval(() => {
    if (ws.readyState !== WebSocket.OPEN) return;
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "ping" }));
    pongTimer = setTimeout(() => ws.close(), timeout); // no pong in time — force the issue
  }, interval);

  return {
    onPong: () => clearTimeout(pongTimer),
    stop: () => { clearInterval(pingTimer); clearTimeout(pongTimer); },
  };
}

The server replies { type: "pong" } to every ping it gets. No reply within the timeout, and you call ws.close() yourself — which hands the problem back to the reconnect loop you already wrote, instead of leaving the app sitting on a socket that looks fine and isn't.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

What "connected" actually means now

Three pieces, each fixing a different lie the green badge was telling: backoff-with-jitter stops reconnects from synchronizing into a storm, a sequence number and a resume handshake stop a clean reconnect from quietly hiding data loss, and an app-level heartbeat stops a socket that's dead from pretending it's fine. None of them are hard individually — the entire reconnect-plus-resume contract is maybe 60 lines. The hard part is noticing that "it reconnects" was never the same claim as "it didn't lose anything," right up until a teammate asks where their message went.

Does your reconnect logic actually ask the server what it missed — or does it just trust the green dot the same way everyone's first version did?
