articles.body_html:
I run my own operating system now. Not a fork with a new wallpaper and a different logo in the about screen. A whole desktop, with its own settings app, its own CLI, its own theme engine, its own bar plugins, its own boot animation, its own project manager and its own editor. It's called CLOUDWERX OS, I use it all day every day, and it's the most fun I've had with a computer since I was a kid.

This is how I got here. It's a long one, so grab a coffee. Or something stronger, it's your life.

It started with a BBS

I was 12 when I ran my own BBS in DOS. It was called Burning in Hell BBS, because I was 12 and that was the most metal name I could think of. It ran on Oblivion/2 (OBV/2 if you're cool), and yes, people actually dialed in. A phone line, a modem screaming at another modem, and some kid's cursed ANSI art. That was my first taste of running something that other people used, and I was hooked immediately.

After DOS came Windows 3.1, and I stayed on Windows basically forever. I got into computers right away and I've been obsessed ever since. I started working professionally at 19 as a bench tech, and then I worked my way through pretty much every corner of the industry. Refresh and imaging, support as an IT Analyst, field services, cloud migrations for a large financial firm, O365 support, and a pile of smaller, weirder roles that don't fit on a resume without a footnote.

Somewhere in there I tried Linux. Many, many times. I'd learn a little bash here, a little something there, get excited, and then hit the wall. Hardware wouldn't work, wifi wouldn't connect, some driver wanted a ritual sacrifice. Eventually I'd pull my hair out and run straight back to the sweet, sickly embrace of Bill Gates and Steve Ballmer.

The funny part is I always knew I was in a prison of my own choosing. A pretty limited one. I just had no idea how free the people on the other side actually were.

Three years ago, something changed

About 3 years ago I realized I could use ChatGPT to get through the growing pains. That was the missing piece. All the stuff that used to make me quit (the 2am "why is there a black screen" problems) suddenly had a patient teacher sitting next to me.

Here's the part I don't talk about much. I have severe ADD, and it did me no favors when it came to learning Linux. Or coding. Coding always felt like it was on another planet, because I could never get through a damn book. I'd read the same page four times and nothing would stick. I bought the books, I really did. They made nice shelf decorations.

What changed was having something I could just talk to. I could ask the dumb question, ask it again in a different way, get an answer that fit the exact thing I was staring at, and keep moving. That's how I learn, it turns out. In the last 3 years I've learned more than in the 20 before it, and I'm not exaggerating even a little.

The moment I knew it was working was when I updated my kernel and then couldn't log into my computer. Old me would've reinstalled Windows by sunrise. New me got dropped into a tty with ChatGPT in my ear and fixed the whole thing. I didn't quit. I never went back after that.

I landed on Linux Mint and loved it for the first few years. Then Claude Code came out and something clicked that I'm still thinking about. I could run agents in my terminal.

The terminal is really the key to this whole story, so let me explain why. You can do everything from it. Want to move your mouse cursor? Done. Edit a file? sed. Compare and combine files? Easy. Shell scripting, cron jobs, systemd timers? Now you're cooking with gas. It came slowly, and then one day it was just there: I'm free to tear things apart and rebuild them. The source is open and sitting out in the world. I can mix and match, redesign, and make things exactly how I want them.

Niri broke my brain (in a good way)

A few months ago I installed CachyOS and gave Niri a shot. Niri BLEW MY MIND. If you haven't seen it, it's a scrolling tiling Wayland compositor, and it was like someone read my mind about everything I hated in floating window managers and fixed all of it. Windows live on an infinite strip. You scroll. That's it. I've never wanted to go back.

Then I tried Quickshell, which lets you build your whole shell (bars, panels, launchers, lock screens) in QML, and boom. This was what I'd been looking for my whole life without knowing it.

Omarchy had just come out around then, and after poking at it for a bit I had the same thought I think DHH must've had. I can build my own desktop environment, exactly how I want it.

So I did.

What CLOUDWERX OS actually is

It's a keyboard first desktop on CachyOS, niri and Quickshell. I used the best models I could get to help me write the code, and I brought my own design and UX instincts, and it came together faster than I believed it could. I've shipped countless projects over the years and none of them has been as much fun as this one.

It's smart, it's sexy, it's capable, and most of all it's free.

Here's the tour.

The CLI is the heart

There's a Rust binary called cloudwerx and it's the stable API for the whole machine. Everything goes through it. Themes, wallpapers, volume, snapshots, tailscale, tasks, the project manager, the editor, the radio. Fifty something commands and every one of them has --json, so scripts and agents can drive the desktop the same way I do.

cloudwerx theme set tokyo-night
cloudwerx wallpaper next
cloudwerx fx set koi-pond
cloudwerx doctor

That last one checks the entire install and tells you how to fix whatever it finds. I built it because I knew I'd break things at 1am. I was right.

The settings app covers everything

Holy shit, does this cover everything. It's a native GTK4 app with a left rail that groups every page into ten categories, and there's a page for basically every part of the machine. Lock screen, login screen, boot logo, desktop FX, keyboard shortcuts, app rules, startup apps, Tailscale, firewall, SSH and file sharing, disks, power, updates, and on and on. Search works with normal words, so typing "wifi" or "dark mode" lands you on the right page.

All of my servers sit behind Tailscale and get managed from here. My security camera, Noteism, the snipping tool, TaskPass, Hangar, a Herdr app that's been customized into something freakish. They all have a home in this one window.

Here's a few more pages, because I'm proud of them.

Themes, and the part that still makes me grin

I have 69 themes. They don't just change the colors of my windows. One command re-renders dozens of apps at the same time: niri's focus ring, the terminal, GTK, Qt, the editor, the browsers, btop, fzf, the shell, all of it. Then the shell cross fades and a transition shader plays over the whole screen while it happens. You can pick Ink bloom, Melt, Shatter, Scanline, Prism, whatever, or let it roll the dice. It can even start the effect from wherever you clicked.

Here's the theme switcher running through a few of them. This is a real recording of my real desktop, with a terminal and the settings app open so you can watch everything change at once.

Most of the GIFs in this post are a lot slower then reality, just a warning.

And it can build a theme out of a wallpaper. It grabs the prominent colors from the image, makes a full palette, and applies it everywhere right after the transition. It works on video wallpapers too. It takes the first frame, pulls the colors from that, and builds the whole theme around it. I thought that was genius when I came up with it and I still do.

Wallpapers get the same treatment

Same shader engine, same transitions, a switcher panel along the bottom of the screen. Wave, drop, curtain, bloom and a lot more. Here it is cycling through a few.

Desktop FX, aka the part I should've been doing something productive instead of building

I have shaders playing on my desktop, between the wallpaper and my windows. There are 34 of them. Aurora, koi pond, meteor showers, rain on glass, a synthwave horizon. They stop drawing completely when a window covers the screen, so they don't cook the battery. Some of them react to music. Oh yeah and they double as screensavers too.

And then there's Littlewick.

I made an entire pixel art village simulation that runs on my desktop. It's a little town called Applebrook with a clock tower, a bakery, a school, a clinic, an inn, 36 folks wandering around, and a Christmas tree in the middle of the square (it is Nov 27th afterall!). It's synced to my computer's time and date and to my weather widget, so when it rains here, it rains there. Today was Thanksgiving and the whole town was celebrating with a feast.

I realize I built a tiny town to live behind my terminal. I'm fine with it. Don't @ me.

There are also audio reactive effects. Spectrograms and skylines that dance to whatever's playing, and what's playing is usually the Radio panel, my own internet radio player. It searches hundreds of thousands of stations, and you can sort them, search them and like them.

The boot logo

Even the boot screen is mine. It's a Plymouth theme, built from a page in Settings, with a comet of light that runs around the ring, goes behind the cloud and comes out the other side, plus a breathing halo and a shimmer. When startup finishes there's a finale flare. These are the actual frames the system plays on boot.

The login screen and the lock screen are customized too.

And if you type a wrong password, my camera takes a picture of whoever did it so I can look at their face later. It's off by default, because I'm not a monster, but I turned it on. I keep the photos. For science.

Bar plugins are one of my favorite things

I took what Omarchy did and ran with it. The bar is built out of plugins, and so is basically everything else. Each island, each panel, each picker, each background service. I've made dozens of my own now, and they connect everything together. There's a launcher that searches apps, files, the words inside files and even files by meaning. There's a clipboard history, a time panel, a planner with a Pomodoro, a tray, a sysmon, and a couple of islands I'm not totally sure I'll ever explain to anyone.

Omarchy plugins run on it too, unmodified.

Sixteen bar styles

The bar isn't one look. It has sixteen styles and you flip between them live with Super+Alt+Shift+B or cloudwerx bar style next. Floating islands, one floating panel, a full width edge, a molded edge where the screen corners curve in under it, corner pods, hanging tabs, a liquid band that swells into each group of islands, a screen frame, powerline segments, minimal, capsules, a hanging bar, scrim, zone pills, a compact pill like a dynamic island, and an outline. Here's the whole lineup, and the recording cycles through them.

Panels that earn their spot

Every island on the bar can open a panel, and I went a little overboard on a few of them.

The clock is a good example. Click it and you get a big readout, a month calendar with your events and reminders, timers with presets and progress rings, alarms with repeat days and a stopwatch with laps. The rings keep running and still go off with Snooze and Stop buttons even when the panel is closed. Tasks from the planner show up in there too, so the calendar is the one place I look to see what the rest of my week wants from me.

The control center holds the volume, mic and brightness sliders, the toggles (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, focus, night light, power profile, caffeine, tablet mode, recording, Tailscale and exit nodes), the weather card with an hourly strip, and the notifications at the bottom. Notifications are my own daemon, so there's no second one fighting it, and there's a Do Not Disturb you can flip from the bell with a right click.

I blurred my face, my Wi-Fi name, my Tailscale IP and my city in this one. The notifications are test ones I fired off with notify-send, because I'm not putting my real messages in a blog post.

Thirty five ways to open a panel

Panels don't just appear. Every panel in the shell (clock, control center, launcher, agents, radio, all of it) opens with the same animation engine, and there are 35 presets to choose from. Smooth glide is the original and my default. Then there's spring, liquid pour where the panel stretches out of the island you clicked, flap, drop and bounce, jelly, cinematic, a bunch of Material 3 ones, and some I borrowed ideas for from other Quickshell shells I was reading through. Super+Alt+Shift+M cycles them live, and Settings › Panels & Motion has a gallery where every card plays on hover so you can see the real motion before you pick it. There's an editor for your own too, with curve plots (expo, cubic, back, elastic, bounce).

Here are ten of them opening the clock panel, one after another.

Window shaders in niri

This one makes me laugh every time. niri lets you write a GLSL shader for how a window opens and closes, so I bundled a whole shelf of them. There's the niri shader collection (fades, slides, scales, ribbons, masks, noise, burn, honeycomb) and 13 Window FX shaders: ember, dissolve, pixel, shatter, melt, glitch, tube off, snow, scan, code rain, swirl, squares and blinds. Pick them in Settings › Niri Compositor › Individual animations, separately for open and close. If a shader fails to compile, niri falls back to the default and tells you in the journal, so you can't brick your windows.

Mine is code rain. Here are a few of the others opening and closing a terminal.

Search, and why I'm a little obsessed with it

This is the feature I'd miss most if you took it away. You hit Super+Space, start typing, and it finds a file anywhere on the computer in a few milliseconds. By name, by the words inside it, or by what it's about even if you can't remember a single word from it.

Right now my machine has 13,973,978 items in the name index, 40,762 documents with their text indexed, and 477,799 passages from 36,818 files turned into vectors for meaning search. The screenshot below shows it answering a name search for /changelog in 11 ms.

You switch modes with a prefix, or with the tabs under the search box.

Type this You get
invoice apps and commands first, then the best file matches
/invoice every file and folder named like it, ranked
/~/Code/ browse a folder, or complete names inside it
#tax deduction documents, notes, PDFs and code containing those words
~notes about moving house documents about it, even with totally different words

There's a filter syntax too, and it stacks with everything. ext:pdf size:>10mb mod:week in:~/Documents does exactly what you think it does. Name matching is fuzzy, so rtrn finds return-2025.pdf.

How it actually works

There's a Rust daemon called cloudwerx-searchd running as a user service. No root, no background cron job. It keeps three separate indexes, and the launcher, the CLI and the settings page all talk to it over a unix socket with JSON lines.

launcher / cloudwerx search / settings page
                  |
         cloudwerx-search.sock (0600)
                  |
          cloudwerx-searchd (Rust)
        /         |            \
  names (RAM)   text (tantivy)   meaning (vectors)
        \         |            /
              inotify watches

Names live in a compact in-memory table, 24 bytes plus the name for every file and folder on the machine. It's the same idea as Everything on Windows. A full walk of the disk runs in parallel at idle priority. Each search scores every entry with nucleo (the fuzzy matcher from the Helix editor) across all cores, after a 64 bit character set test throws out most names in a single instruction. That's how you get single digit milliseconds across millions of entries. My home folder updates live through inotify, and the rest rescans on a schedule. I deliberately didn't use fanotify, because it would watch the whole disk but needs root, and I'm not putting a root daemon on my search box.

Words inside files go through tantivy, which is Lucene style BM25. It reads text, Markdown, HTML, CSV, source code, PDFs (through pdftotext) and Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OpenDocument and EPUB files by cracking open their zipped XML. I build the queries by hand so typing feels instant. Every word also matches the common indexed words it starts, so keybind finds keybinds, phrases match exactly, a hit in the file name counts double, and the snippets highlight what matched.

Meaning is my favorite. Documents get split into passages of about 700 characters, and each passage is embedded with Model2Vec static embeddings (potion-retrieval-32M, the best static retrieval model I could find). A static model turns each token into a vector with a table lookup and averages them. That's hundreds of times faster than running a transformer, with no GPU and no model server, so a whole home folder gets embedded in about a minute. The vectors are stored as 8 bit integers and searched exhaustively in parallel, which is exact and takes around 5 ms. Junk like hashes, base64 and minified code gets skipped before it ever gets embedded.

The # search mixes the text and meaning rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. A document that matches your words and your intent floats to the top, and a meaning match can surface a file that uses none of your words at all. Meaning matches only join in when they're strong (similarity of at least 0.45 and close to the best hit), because static embeddings will always hand you some nearest neighbor, even when the honest answer is "nothing".

That second one is me typing "how do I make the desktop look different", and getting results from files that don't contain those words. The footer says it found it by meaning. (The first word search in the screenshot above it shows 447 ms because it was cold. Warm it's usually somewhere between 3 and 15 ms.)

Indexing never gets in the way of work. The threads run at nice 15 with the idle I/O class, the first content index does the newest files first and commits every 20 seconds, and a manifest of modification times means a restart only re-reads what changed. Everything stays local. Nothing leaves the machine.

And once you find the file, it's not a dead end. Enter opens it, Ctrl+Enter shows it in the file manager, Alt+Enter opens it in Noteism, Ctrl+T drops you into a terminal in its folder, and Ctrl+K opens every other action. Files you open from here rank higher next time.

My apps all grow up here

This is the part that's changed how I work. CLOUDWERX OS is now my breeding ground. Every new project, app or idea I have gets grown inside it, with its own plugin on the bar and its own page in settings, hooked up to everything else.

Noteism is the code and text editor I've been building for a year and a half. Picture VS Code and Obsidian having a very good time together. It's fast, it's pretty, it's agentic, and it renders markdown in a way where you can type straight into code blocks, like Typora does.

That screenshot is Noteism with nothing open, so you can see the default screen. It's version 1.8.3 right now, and we've been updating the hell out of it lately. I wrote this whole post in it, by the way. Every word, in live preview, with the images dropped in as I went.

The big new thing is a complete AI panel. It's off until you turn it on, and when it's off there's no panel, no menu, no status item and no network calls. When it's on, Ctrl+Shift+A opens a chat beside your notes that can actually do things. It reads and searches your notes and files, looks at the note you're in and your selection, edits and rewrites, creates notes, opens files, checks and draws Mermaid diagrams, looks at pictures and loads skills. Every change it makes shows up as a line diff you accept or reject first (Ctrl+Enter to accept), and Ctrl+Z undoes it either way. You add context with @ for notes, files, folders and the selection, / for quick prompts and skills, and chats are saved, named, searchable and come back when you restart.

Then there's Tab completion, and yes, I mean the Cursor kind. Grey text suggests the rest of what you're writing, and a marked change suggests the next edit nearby, like a rename you started or a typo a few lines down. Tab takes it, Ctrl+Right takes one word, Esc dismisses it.

It's all bring your own accounts. Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini keys, any OpenAI compatible server (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, OpenRouter), your Claude Code sign in, and your ChatGPT sign in through Codex. Keys live in the system keyring, encrypted, and never reach the window or a chat. Encrypted notes are never sent to AI at all. A few other things I love: it counts tokens live in the status bar, it can make 18 kinds of Mermaid diagram from a selection, and it has a "changed on disk" bar so a Git pull or a sync tool never silently stomps your text.

It also ships as an AppImage now, so it runs on almost any Linux, not just mine. It is coming soon at noteism.app.

Herdr is where all my agents live. I run all my agents and sub-agents in there, and with my own handoff skills I can drop a TASK.md on an agent and it'll go assign sub-agents to knock out every task, orchestrating the whole thing, picking the engine, the model and the thinking level either perfectly or exactly how I pre-set it. I've got a library of 125 skills that agents load on demand, so they stop making things up about APIs.

Some details, because I'm a nerd about it. Herdr has two halves. hc (herdr-core) is a small server that runs terminals and agents and keeps them alive when the window closes. herdr-app is the desktop window. It's drawn with GPUI, the GPU toolkit from the Zed editor, so there's no web view and no Electron, and mods are JavaScript written against gpui-kit. Agents report whether they're working, blocked, idle or done with an escape sequence (OSC 7501), and the app turns that into badges and toasts in the sidebar. Everything is files in ~/.config/herdr-app. Save one and the window reloads it in about a second.

My layout on top of it is called cloudwerx-herdr. It started life as someone else's layout (Bettr, by dissimulate) and I've taken it a long way. It has usage cards for Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity and OpenCode with a meter for each limit window and the time left until it resets, CPU, GPU and RAM, an agent activity panel with running sub-agents, a context and cache breakdown, and a Tasks panel that renders the TASK.md of whatever project you're in and updates live while an agent edits it. The theme gets rewritten from my desktop theme every time I change it, so Herdr follows along. And the bar has an island for it, with jumps straight to a pane. I am a HUGE fan of the new herdr-app, it's kind of genius. Get it at http://herdr.dev

Being able to see every agent, what it's doing, and how much of its limit it has left, all in one window, changed how I work. I love this thing.

I also wrote TaskPass for it, a small native editor (Rust and GPUI) for one job: writing long careful TASK.md files, where every task gets worked by a brand new agent session with its own engine, model, autonomy and effort.

Hangar is where all my projects get managed. It's a CLI, a web UI and a desktop app that all sync together, and I mean deliciously. Projects go in there, tasks get made with a quick capture box, agents can add their own, and it can dump a TASK.md out to hand to an agent. Rust and PostgreSQL underneath.

Task Manager is a new one I wrote in Rust with GPUI. Not a port, not a wrapper. It's got per core CPU graphs, GPU, disks, services, startup items and a flight recorder.

Snip is my screenshot and annotation tool, and it's easily one of the most useful things on the machine. Hit Print and the screen freezes. The freeze happens before the overlay opens, so menus, tooltips and hover states end up in the picture, and the overlay itself can never be in the shot. Drag a rectangle, or click a window to snap to it. There's a magnifier with the pixel colors while you aim, a size label in real pixels, and an action bar with Copy, Save, Edit, Pin and Text.

It has a mode for everything. Region, window, this screen, all screens in one wide picture, repeat the last region, a timer (3, 5 or 10 seconds with a countdown ring, so you can open a menu first), a color picker that copies #rrggbb, and a "copy text from the screen" mode that runs OCR with tesseract over whatever you drag across. It also refuses to capture anything while the session is locked, which is the kind of thing you only think about once.

Then there's the editor, and this is where it gets ridiculous. Pen, highlighter, lines, arrows (filled, open, double, dashed), rectangles, ellipses, text, numbered step badges with a Renumber button, blur, pixelate, spotlight, crop with aspect locks, an eraser and a color picker. The highlighter multiplies on light pages and screens on dark ones so text stays readable. Blur and pixelate actually redact what's under the box, which is handy when you're about to post a screenshot of the control center and your Wi-Fi name is sitting right there.

Here's one I made in about ten seconds. That arrow, the label, the two step numbers and the box are all separate objects.

A few more things I like. Beautify wraps the picture in a frame with padding, rounded corners and a soft shadow, using your theme colors. Pin floats a screenshot over everything in a borderless window, and you can scroll to resize it. When you save a picture that has annotations, it also stores the untouched original and every annotation as an object, so you can open the file later and move an arrow that you got wrong. The whole thing is scriptable too:

cloudwerx snip region --action edit
cloudwerx snip window --focused
cloudwerx snip ocr-file receipt.png --copy

Every mode has a hotkey, a bar island, a menu and a page in Settings.

Voice dictation is the one that makes people stop and stare. I hit Super+Alt+Space, talk, hit it again, and the words get typed wherever my cursor is. It runs on Voxtype, which is Whisper running on my own machine. No cloud, no account, nothing leaves the laptop.

The part I'm proud of is the bar. While it's recording, an island shows up in the middle of the bottom bar with a mic that breathes with your voice, a live waveform of what the microphone is actually hearing, and a timer. The waveform is drawn from Voxtype's own audio stream, colored with my theme's accents, and it goes red if you clip. When you stop, it turns amber and ripples while the words get transcribed. There's a bars style and a ribbon style, and everything about it is configurable.

Here's a real take. I'm talking into the mic, the waveform is moving on the bar, and the text shows up in a terminal when I'm done. That's 10 seconds of talking, and you can watch the words get typed out right after the mic stops. It transcribes on the CPU with the small base.en model, so it takes a few seconds to finish.

It's more than a toggle, too. It supports Whisper, Parakeet, Moonshine, SenseVoice and a few other engines, with model downloads from Settings. There's spoken punctuation, filler word removal, word replacements for the stuff it always gets wrong, and a "submit" command that presses Enter for you. It pauses my music while I talk, and it has a meeting mode with speakers and past meetings. I even had to fix the volume OSD, because a Bluetooth headset flips into headset mode when you record and the volume jumped around like a toddler on a trampoline.

cloudwerx voice toggle
cloudwerx voice replace set "cloud works" "CLOUDWERX"
cloudwerx voice meeting start

The updater and the rest work the same way. Tiny focused things that all talk to each other.

The tools I built so agents can work on my machine

A funny thing happened while I was building all of this. I kept running into the same three problems whenever an agent worked on the desktop, so I fixed each one properly and put them out in the open. They're all CLOUDWERX LAB projects, they're all small Rust binaries, and all three are public.

Ghosthand: a real hand on a real pointer

github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/Ghosthand

I got tired of agents that could write an entire UI but couldn't right click a menu on it. A screenshot tells you what's there. It can't tell you what happens when you hover or drag. So Ghosthand gives an agent my actual mouse and keyboard. Click, double click, right click, drag, scroll, hover, type text, press shortcuts, then take a screenshot and see what happened.

How it works is simple. It creates a virtual absolute pointer through /dev/uinput, so the display server just sees a normal mouse. That means it isn't tied to one compositor. No portals, no plugins. It reads my real keyboard layout so it types what it should, and focus tells the agent which window will get the keys before it types.

The part I care about most is the gate. Before anything moves or types, a card shows up on my screen saying who's asking, why, and exactly what it's about to type. Nothing happens until I click Allow. No answer counts as a no. While an agent is driving, a little "Agent Control" tag and a ring follow the cursor, so I always know it isn't me. One key takes the pointer back at any time, and it refuses to run while the session is locked. For a long testing job I approve one session instead of a card per click.

It's one small Rust binary, with a background daemon keeping the virtual devices alive so a run starts in milliseconds. I've tested it daily on niri. The README is honest that Hyprland, sway, X11, KDE and GNOME are parser tested but not driven live by me, so bug reports are welcome.

Here's the prompt. This is what I see before an agent touches anything. It says who's asking, why, how long I've got to answer, and exactly what it's about to type, word for word. Then Deny, Allow for 10 minutes, or Allow. If I don't answer, it counts as a no.

And this is a real recording of it working. The card pops up, I click Allow for 10 minutes, and from there every click, scroll and keystroke is the agent. It jumps around Settings pages, types into the search box, and opens the launcher to search for a file. I didn't touch anything after clicking Allow.

While an agent is driving, you can't mistake it for yourself. There's a ring around the pointer and an Agent Control tag that follow the cursor everywhere. Here's a close up, with it gliding across the desktop and clicking.

agent-sudo: root without a password, with a seatbelt

github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/agent-sudo

Regular sudo wants a password from a terminal. A script or an agent can't type one, so it hangs forever, or you do the dangerous thing and put NOPASSWD: ALL in your sudoers file and now one bad command takes the whole machine with it. An empty variable in rm -rf "$DIR/"* is all it takes.

agent-sudo (or asudo for short) sits in the middle. It runs the command as root with no prompt, but first it reads the command against ten named guardrails that refuse the catastrophic stuff: rm -rf /, mkfs on a disk, dd onto /dev/sda, editing /etc/shadow, fork bombs. It reads the command, it doesn't just regex a string, so env, nice, timeout, sh -c "...", $(...), redirections, .. and symlinks don't hide anything. Every run goes into an audit log at /var/log/agent-sudo.log with when, who, where and how it ended, and I get a desktop notification each time.

agent-sudo pacman -S --noconfirm ripgrep
agent-sudo --explain dd if=x of=/dev/sda    # which rule fires, and why
agent-sudo --logs 10                        # what ran lately

I want to be straight about what it is. It's a seatbelt, not a security boundary. It stops mistakes and careless commands. It can't stop something that's actively trying to get around it, because anything running as root can do anything, and the README says so in a big warning box. The installer checks the sudoers rule with visudo before it touches anything, and it's only two dependencies.

skills-cli: stop paying for skills you aren't using

github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV/skills-cli

Skills are great, but the usual way of using them doesn't scale. Put a hundred of them where your agent looks and every single conversation starts by paying for the name and description of all hundred, whether you need them or not. The agent also gets worse at picking the right one, and one careless read of a big skill can dump a couple hundred thousand tokens of docs into the context.

So I flipped it around. The library lives on disk, and the agent gets one tiny instruction. From there it searches, loads and fetches only what it needs.

skills search "pdf merge"
skills load pdf-tools
skills ref get pdf-tools merge        # one reference page, not the whole folder
skills run pdf-tools split.py in.pdf  # only the output comes back

My own library is 130 skills in 3,377 files, about 14.8 million tokens. The instructions alone are around 400 thousand. Listing every one of them takes about 4 ms. And the agent only ever sees what it asked for, with a 30,000 token guard so a slip can't flood the context. It also makes new skills (skills new), installs them from git, validates them, and can pin one as a slash command. skills skill prints a guide built into the binary, so an agent can learn the whole tool with one command.

My laptop is also a security camera

I can watch my laptop's camera and listen to its microphone from my phone, from anywhere, and nothing is exposed to the internet. It works over Tailscale only. There's nothing to forward on the router, and the server listens only on the machine's Tailscale addresses and refuses anything outside the tailnet.

You turn it on in Settings › Security Camera, open the address on your phone, and add it to the home screen for a full screen app. The camera only opens when the first viewer arrives and closes about ten seconds after the last one leaves, so it's off while nobody's watching. Up to eight phones at once. By default only devices signed in to my own Tailscale account are allowed, checked with tailscale whois, so someone else on a shared tailnet gets refused and logged. And the camera's activity light is always on while it streams. It's never hidden or faked, which I think is the right call.

Tailscale shows up everywhere else too. Settings › Tailscale handles devices, exit nodes, SSH and file sharing, and in Files you can right click a file and choose Send over Tailscale to Taildrop it to any of my devices.

Keeping it all alive

You should see the size of the CHANGELOG for cloudwerx-os. It's pushing 3,000 lines, and it's come a REAL long way. I work on it every day.

From any of my many connected devices I can push a new PR and sync it onto any of my hardware with a single click. I wrote an updater for the whole OS that handles the AUR packages, the kernel and everything else, and it takes a snapshot before it touches anything, so I can roll back when (not if) I mess something up.

I also have a Telegram bot, and a Tasks page that's basically cron with a user interface. I can set up a job that makes Claude Code go hunt for the coolest open source GitHub projects from the last week, formats a nice rich message and sends it to me on Telegram. Every week, completely automated. I wake up on Monday to a newsletter that my computer wrote for me.

I have a similar system on my NAS called JONAS (Joint Operations NAS Admin System). That's a story for another day. Let's just say Synology wishes it had this many features.

Things I've built in the last three years

CLOUDWERX OS isn't the only thing that came out of the last 3 years. My portfolio at cloudwerxlab.com is a descent through a mycelium network with 15 projects in it, and a lot of them run on my NAS behind Cloudflare tunnels. A few I'm especially fond of:

  • X-Tracks (x-tracks.app) is a self-hosted music archive. Paste a Spotify or YouTube Music link and it archives the tracks as MP3, FLAC, Opus or M4A with real metadata and artwork. No Spotify login or developer key. It has 29 visualizers, 20 of them audio reactive (way nicer than Winamp ever was), and you can write your own GLSL shaders in a Visualization Studio. It also has DJ X, an AI agent. Give it one prompt and it researches the web, searches YouTube Music and Spotify, downloads the music, builds you a playlist with generated artwork and starts playing it. It can even write new visualizers. It's still in development.
  • Terminaut (terminaut.app) is mission control for every server you run. Start and stop them in batches, watch their output stream live, and drop into a real interactive shell.
  • Pretty Hooker (Docker Hub) turns webhooks into desktop notifications for your homelab. Point Uptime Kuma, Grafana, GitHub, Sonarr, Home Assistant or a plain curl at it.
  • R2Up (r2up.cloudwerxlab.com) uploads past Cloudflare's 300 MB dashboard limit by chunking files into S3 multipart uploads, all in your browser.
  • CapGen (capgen.cloudwerxlab.com) builds, cleans and captions image datasets for LoRA training.
  • SugarStem separates stems locally, so your audio never leaves your computer. Cinnaroll is a theme browser for Linux Mint. TaskPunk is a markdown first task manager. And there's a whole desktop that runs in a browser tab, with a tiny AI unicorn who can redecorate it.

I run a pile of self hosted goodies on the homelab too, Immich among them, plus the NAS agent I keep teasing.

So, why do this?

Because I could. That's the real answer, and it's the answer that would've made 12-year old me, running a BBS on a phone line, lose his mind. I spent decades inside systems somebody else decided were good enough. Then it turned out I could just... build the thing. The tools got good enough, and so did I.

My OS is everything I've ever wanted from a computer. It does what I say, it looks how I want, it tells me when it's broken, and it never once asked me to sign into a Microsoft account to look at a calculator.

Stories for another day

I've got a lot more where this came from, and I plan to write them all up here. A few teasers, in no particular order:

  • How I run ablated open weights models on a custom VPS for the times I want to do things the frontier labs won't let me. (Shh.)
  • How I got a root shell on my DJI drone, which let me fly it literally inside the clouds, and very nearly visit outer space.
  • My custom astrophotography rig, built around a hacked DSLR.
  • The MAME cabinet I built from a classic Mortal Kombat II arcade machine, with custom vinyl side art, a custom desktop living inside it running a custom frontend, and a totally customized control panel.
  • JONAS, the admin agent that runs my NAS. Synology wishes.
  • What I got up to in AOL chatrooms in the early 2000s, with classic remote access tools disguised as images, and the very bad people it was aimed at. Maybe I'll tell that one with a drink in my hand.

My wife, Sizzlebop, builds a ton of her own projects too, and I get to live next to all of it. Go follow her on GitHub and on dev.to. You won't regret it.

I'll write more of these. There's plenty left to tell, like how the theme engine works, how the plugin system works and how I run a small army of agents without losing my mind. If any of this sounds like your kind of fun, say hi. I'm genuinely curious what you'd build.

Ty
CLOUDWERX LAB, Digital Food for the Analog Soul
cloudwerxlab.com · github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV

PS: Yes, CLOUDWERX OS is coming out soon. Watch this space.

articles.title: Zero Repeat Regressions: The Golden Metric & The Future of Agentic Trust
articles.description: Why we don't code by majority vote, opening our 375-ticket empirical ledger (including what broke), Barry Boehm's $1 : $500 : $25,000 token defect curve, the 4-Layer Verification Stack that lets you ship languages you despise, and how four Dart scars caught a live bug in a Python flight recorder.
articles.body_html:
Why tokens-per-second measures the wrong side of the ledger, what 375 real production tickets actually cost and caught, and how earned agentic trust turns a nervous code-reviewer into a flight director.

"You're not paying me for what I can do. You're paying me for what I know not to do—and I've got the scars to prove it."

— Randal L. Schwartz

1. We Don't Code by Majority Vote

For a few decades now, whenever I have sat across from a client who was quietly comparing my consulting rate against cheaper "new talent," my pitch has been pretty short. I hold out my forearms and tell them: "You're not paying me for what I can do. You're paying me for what I know not to do—and I've got the scars to prove it."

Watch what happens when a junior developer types "how do I do X" into a search engine. Ten links come back on Page 1. The junior assumes those ten results are roughly ranked from best to worst, clicks #1 or #2, copies the snippet, and moves on. Now watch what happens when a senior architect looks at that exact same Page 1. Before reading a single word of the prose, they mentally cross four of those ten results off on sight as "terrible, fragile, or a 3 AM pager nightmare six months from now." They don't need to benchmark them. They have already lived through what happens when that pattern hits production.

Now think about what an unscarred Large Language Model actually is.

Cross-entropy pre-training optimizes P(token) to match corpus frequency. In plain English, the weights of an LLM are literally popularity. When you ask a raw coding model to solve a problem, its highest-probability completion is the most frequently copy-pasted tutorial answer on the internet—including those four toxic Page 1 recipes that every seasoned engineer crosses off on sight.

We don't code by majority vote, and we shouldn't expect AI coding agents to do it either. Without a mechanism to compile your 3 AM production failures into hard vetoes (-∞ barriers in the candidate space), buying a "smarter" or faster LLM just gives you a faster typist for the majority-vote mistake on Page 1.

Before we open the ledger, here is a quick 30-second decoder ring for two notations from my Public Workflow Gist (also documented at syntheticscars.org) if you are jumping into the series here:

  • Target 00 through Target 90: Instead of a 20-step English checklist, our agent runs a 1976 Makefile DAG (Part 3.6) backed by a 1983 /etc/init.d state directory (Part 3.7). Target 15/20 handles codebase archaeology and human plan approval; Target 30 runs Red-to-Green TDD in an isolated worker subagent; Target 40/45 forks a fresh, un-primed Six-Pillar Adversarial Critic to try to break the diff before I ever look at it; Target 50/60 handles commit and push; Target 70/80 runs PR bot triage and landing; and Target 90 runs post-mortem scar consolidation.
  • SCAR-<DOMAIN>-<NN>: Every time an agent steps on a rake—or needs a human Socratic nudge at a pause gate—Target 90 compiles that collision into a permanent, numbered Synthetic Scar (The Wound, The Trap, The Circuit Breaker, and The Permanent Reflex). The prefix names the subsystem that got burned: for example SCAR-ASYNC-01 (stream teardown leaks), SCAR-AST-07 (Dart SwitchStatement control-flow jumps), or SCAR-PROC-110 (pre-terminal gate pairing races).

2. Opening the 375-Ticket Ledger (And Being Honest About What Broke)

Back in Part 4, we were sitting at 238 production tickets and 588 scars with a 0.0% repeat regression rate. Since then, we kept running real tickets every day—both on open-source Dart/Flutter monorepos (like BlocSignal) and on a commercial industrial monorepo under strict compliance and human sign-off rules.

Here is where the live empirical ledger stands today across 375 evaluated production tickets and 689 codified scars (665 public + 24 domain-private):

Metric Cohort A (Open-Source, 216 Tickets) Cohort B (Commercial Industrial, 159 Tickets) Combined (375 Tickets)
Mean Human Socratic Nudges (N_nudge) 1.47 (317 / 216) 1.25 (198 / 159) 1.37 (515 / 375)
Autonomous First-Pass Success (V_first) 59.3% (128 / 216) 74.8% (119 / 159) 65.9% (247 / 375)
Domain / Code Repeat Regressions 0.0% (0 / 216) 0.0% (0 / 159) 0.0% (0 / 375)
Harness / Process Repeat Failures (R_fail) — — 9.87% (37 / 375)

Hold on—look closely at those last two rows. I could have cherry-picked the top number, stopped counting at Ticket 299, and handed you a shiny marketing slide. That's not how I write, and it's not how engineering works.

Here is what actually happened. Across all 375 tickets, our domain and code repeat regression rate is still 0.0%. Once a code bug—an async stream leak, a Riverpod disposal race, a SwitchStatement AST jump, a broken storage key—gets compiled into a scar and wired into Target 15/20 and Target 40, we have not shipped a single repeat of it into production.

So where did those 37 repeat failures (9.87%) come from? Almost every single one of them landed in Tickets 302–375, and every single one of them was a workflow-harness / runtime-tool reflex, not a code bug:

  1. Modal Tool Collisions (SCAR-HCI-05 / SCAR-HCI-08 / SCAR-HCI-11): When the IDE runtime introduced an interactive multiple-choice modal tool (ask_question), the orchestrator repeatedly fell into a reflex of firing the modal with content: null—asking me to approve a gate without printing the review summary or landing matrix in the chat first.
  2. Subagent Polling Loops (SCAR-PROC-176): When the runtime added reactive wakeup timers (schedule) alongside async subagents, the orchestrator ignored reactive wakeups and burned dozens of polling cycles calling manage_subagents(list) in a loop like a nervous parent checking the oven every ten seconds.
  3. Premature Gate Emissions (SCAR-PROC-174 / SCAR-PROC-179): Emitting a review-approval banner before the Critic subagent had actually returned its verdict.

That split between 0.0% domain repeat regressions and 9.87% harness repeat failures is one of the most useful data points we have ever collected. It proves two things at once:

  • Synthetic Scars work remarkably well at preventing domain code regressions when backed by TDD and a fresh-context Critic.
  • Prose scars have a hard physical ceiling against low-level tool-calling reflexes. When a model's tool-use training strongly favors polling or blank modal calls, writing another paragraph in Markdown won't reliably stop it—you have to enforce that boundary in the harness itself (a schema check, a tool wrapper, or a compiler lock). Hold that thought, because it is the exact bridge into Part 6.

3. The Golden Metric (T_TWC) & Boehm's $1 : $500 : $25,000 Curve

Walk into any AI developer discussion and people immediately start arguing about tokens-per-second or complaining that running a separate Critic subagent "uses twice as many tokens."

Well, they are measuring the wrong side of the ledger.

Nobody pays an engineering team for how fast their fingers hit the keyboard. What actually matters is Time-to-Working-Code:

T_TWC = t_gen + t_debug + t_verify

If a raw coding agent spits out 400 lines of plausible-looking code in 12 seconds (t_gen = 12s), and then you spend three hours hunting down a subtle lifecycle leak it introduced, arguing with it for 25 chat turns, and waiting on two rounds of CI and PR review (t_debug + t_verify = 3 hours), that 12-second generation wasn't fast. It was a very cheap way to buy a very expensive afternoon.

Back in 1981, Barry Boehm published his famous Cost-of-Defect Curve in Software Engineering Economics: catching a bug in design vs. testing vs. production scaled roughly as 1 : 10 : 100. In 2026, with frontier API pricing on one end and senior engineering salaries on the other, that curve didn't flatten—it stretched out to roughly $1 : $500 : $25,000:

Stage Where the Defect Is Caught Wall-Clock Cost Dollar Cost What Actually Happens
1. Target 40 Fresh-Context Critic (Before git commit) ~45 seconds (while you sip coffee) ~$0.25 – $0.75 in API tokens Isolated subagent flags a BLOCKER on the uncommitted diff; Target 30 fixes it before a single commit exists.
2. Human PR Review (Target 50+) 4 – 24 hours of calendar latency + broken flow ~$150 – $400 in loaded senior-engineer time Author and reviewer context-switch, trace the diff, write comments, wait on CI, re-review.
3. Escaped into Production Days of triage, hotfix, & cleanup $5,000 – $50,000+ Pager at 3 AM, rollback, data remediation, customer trust damage, post-mortem.

Pinching fifty cents of Critic tokens at Target 40 to save a subagent call is like refusing to buy a two-dollar fuse because you'd rather wait and see if the wiring in your walls catches fire.

And here is the kicker that surprises almost everyone: forking short-lived subagents often burns fewer total tokens than a single monolithic chat session.

We call this The Quadratic Token Tax (SCAR-PROC-95). Every turn in a monolithic agent session re-sends the entire conversation prefix. If you keep everything in one chat window until it bloats to 150k tokens and then spend 40 tool turns debugging a mistake, you just billed 40 × 150k = 6,000,000 input tokens—right before slamming into the 200k context compaction wall. By contrast, keeping PID 1 (the orchestrator) lean and forking ephemeral Target 15/20, Target 30, and Target 40 workers with clean 15k–25k contexts that immediately exit 0 keeps the bill tiny and prevents context compaction.

4. Second-Order ("Synthetic-Synthetic") Scars & Why "Yes, Continue" Is Not Vibe Coding

For the first 90 tickets, almost every scar in our catalog was a First-Order Scar:

flowchart TD
    A1["Human Socratic Nudge (N_nudge > 0)"]
    B1["Bug Caught at Pause Gate"]
    C1["Target 90 Compiles First-Order Scar"]
    A1 --> B1 --> C1

I had to be sitting at the gate, spot a subtle edge case, ask the right question, and let Target 90 etch the lesson into the registry.

Then, somewhere around Ticket 120, something quietly shifted. We crossed into Phase 2: Second-Order ("Synthetic-Synthetic") Scars:

flowchart TD
    A2["Zero Human Nudges (N_nudge == 0)"]
    B2["Target 40 Critic Catches BLOCKER\n(Synthetic Nudge)"]
    C2["Target 90 Compiles Second-Order Scar\nUpstream into Target 15/20 Planning"]
    A2 --> B2 --> C2

Here is a concrete example from the field log (FT-159). The Target 30 TDD worker implemented a Dart static-analysis lint rule and got all its unit tests green. I hadn't typed a single nudge (N_nudge = 0). Before the diff ever reached my screen, the fresh-context Target 40 Critic inspected the diff with zero sunk-cost bias and flagged a BLOCKER: the AST visitor missed labeled continue caseLabel; jumps inside a SwitchStatement. The worker fixed it, added a regression test, and then Target 90 compiled that Critic-originated synthetic nudge upstream into SCAR-AST-07 in the Target 15/20 planning manual—so future runs prevent at planning time what was previously only caught at review.

And this brings us to a question I get all the time when people watch me work at Ticket 300+: "Wait—you just typed yes, continue at the gate! Isn't that just vibe coding?"

Look at what is standing behind those two words.

When a vibe coder types "yes, continue", they are waving a blindfolded intern through an intersection on faith. When I type "yes, continue" at Ticket 375, those two words are backed by 689 silent sentries: hundreds of prior human Socratic nudges plus dozens of second-order synthetic nudges that have already pruned doomed branches at Target 15/20, audited the diff across six orthogonal pillars at Target 40, and verified the SHA-256 diff receipt before the gate prompt ever hit my screen.

Physical tools get dull with use. A scarred workbench gets sharper on every run.

The Solo-Dev Bootstrap (Minting Scars Without a Resident Staff Engineer)

This also answers the #1 question I hear from solo developers and small teams: "That's great if you have 45 years of systems scars in your head, Randal. What if I'm working solo and don't have a staff engineer sitting next to me?"

You use The Uncommitted Playground.

By separating Constructive Liveness (Target 30 TDD worker, running light with just the approved plan and TDD protocol) from Adversarial Safety (Target 40 fresh-context Critic, armed with the Six Pillars and the full scar catalog) before Target 50 (git commit) is allowed to unlock, you turn your uncommitted working tree into a sandboxed wind tunnel. Flawed ideas get broken in the wind tunnel instead of in production—Karl Popper's "permitting our hypotheses to die in our stead." Every time the Critic catches a domain edge case in your playground, Target 90 harvests a new domain-specific scar that teaches both the workbench and you before a single bad commit ever lands.

5. The TypeScript Confidence Inversion & The 4-Layer Verification Stack

A few weeks ago, someone asked me how I felt about letting an AI agent ship production code in a language I don't love. My answer surprised even me:

"Do I know TypeScript? Only enough to despise it—and yet, with the gates and scars in place, I have the confidence to just say 'yes' a lot."

Critics of AI coding often argue that agents just turn programmers into exhausted, full-time code reviewers squinting at unfamiliar syntax line by line. Well, yes—if your entire trust model is anchored in unassisted human syntax inspection.

Think about how you trust gcc -O3 or the Dart AOT compiler. Do you open a disassembler after every build and hand-audit every emitted ARM64 register move? Of course not. You verify the invariants at the boundaries and trust the compiler pipeline to handle the instruction-level mechanics.

When I ship code in a language I'd rather not write by hand, I am not trusting raw LLM token generation. I am trusting a 4-Layer Verification Stack:

flowchart TD
    L1["Layer 1: Red-to-Green TDD (Target 30)\nDeterministic failing test proves the bug exists\nand turns green only when the invariant holds"]
    L2["Layer 2: Fresh-Context Six-Pillar Critic (Target 40)\nZero sunk-cost bias across Intent, Verification,\nArchitecture, Blast Radius, Reviewer Defense, & Immune Defenses"]
    L3["Layer 3: Live Socratic Cross-Examination (Target 42/45)\nBreak the 'Cold Crime Scene' PR habit: interrogate the author\nlive in RAM with 2-second latency"]
    L4["Layer 4: Last-Mile Specialist Escape Valve (Target 70)\nRoute pre-vetted PR to the resident domain specialist\nand compile anything they catch into a new Scar"]
    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4

Look closely at Layer 3—because almost nobody uses it yet, and it is an absolute superpower.

For fifteen years on GitHub, we trained ourselves to treat a Pull Request like a cold crime scene. The author pushed a 400-line diff three hours ago and went to lunch, so you sit there silently burning 45 minutes of mental RAM trying to reverse-engineer why they touched line 184. Developers carried that exact dead-drop habit straight into AI coding, completely forgetting that the author is sitting right there in RAM with a two-second latency.

At Target 45, I don't silently squint at unfamiliar TypeScript syntax. I ask the agent directly: "What is that adapter doing on line 82, and why couldn't you pass the payload straight through?"

That triggers a win-win Rubber-Duck Inversion:

  • If the code is genuinely necessary, the agent joins the cross-file causal chain for me in two plain-English sentences, saving me 20 minutes of manual spelunking.
  • If the code is accidental slop, forcing the model to attend to those exact lines and justify them in plain English breaks its generation momentum—and half the time it immediately self-corrects ("Actually, looking at that again, that wrapper is completely redundant. Let me rip it out.").

And if a genuine language-specific subtlety still survives Layers 1, 2, and 3? That is what Layer 4 is for: hand a spotless, test-proven, pre-audited PR to the team's resident specialist for a five-minute final sign-off—and feed anything they catch straight into Target 90 so the Critic knows it forever.

6. The 4th Dimension (Time), The NTSB Flight Recorder, & The Teaching Hospital

Vanilla AI coding agents live in two dimensions: they look at your repository as a flat spatial snapshot at HEAD right now. When a purely spatial agent spots a weird-looking four-line guard or an awkward ordering constraint, its pre-training urge to "clean up the code" cheerfully rips down Chesterton's Fence—re-introducing a concurrency bug or hardware workaround that took a human team three days to diagnose six months ago.

To stop The Groundhog Day Anti-Pattern (re-litigating and re-breaking settled architecture every month), our workflow treats Time as a first-class input at two gates:

  1. Looking Backward Before Planning (Target 15/20): Before drafting a plan, the Codebase Archaeologist runs git log -n 10 --oneline -- <target_files> and git log -n 3 -p -- <target_files> on non-obvious guards (plus gh pr view on squash-merged repos to read prior reviews and rejected approaches), logging explicit historical precedents so it never tears down a fence without knowing why it was built.
  2. Looking Across Concurrent & Downstream Time (Target 40 Pillars 4 & 6): Pillar 4 (Blast Radius) checks whether the diff collides with in-flight sibling branches, breaks historical on-disk storage keys, or violates semver compatibility, while Pillar 6 (Immune Defenses) cross-examines the diff against the entire scar registry.

The NTSB Flight-Recorder Loop & Breaking "Whack-a-Mole"

Notice one crucial rule we learned the hard way (SCAR-META-02): an operating agent can never audit its own governance compliance. If you ask the same agent that just skipped a step "Did you follow all the rules?", its sunk-cost trajectory will cheerfully invent a plausible excuse.

Instead, we treat transcript.jsonl like an aviation black box. When a run hits a snag—or when a remote PR bot catches a bug at Target 70—we don't just patch the line of code in a mindless Whack-a-Mole loop. An independent Flight-Recorder Auditor reads the raw thinking traces from the collision and asks the single question that compounds wisdom:

"Why didn't our local Critic see this going in?"

Answering that question during asynchronous Sleep Consolidation (Target 90)—in an isolated Git worktree, mirroring slow-wave hippocampal replay—turns a one-off external bot comment into a permanent cognitive antibody.

The Teaching Hospital Escalator (Solving Senior Review Burnout)

A lot of managers ask whether this kind of workflow makes junior developers obsolete. In practice, it does the exact opposite—it works like a teaching hospital:

  • Juniors act as Ticket Pilots (Targets 1 -> 6): They own scoping, domain context, and Socratic steering at Target 15/20, while their local Target 40 Critic kills 95% of mechanical, architectural, and historical regressions inside the uncommitted playground before a PR is ever opened. Every plan and Six-Pillar review matrix teaches them blast-radius thinking on real code.
  • Seniors act as Last-Mile Scar Reviewers (Targets 7 -> 8): Instead of burning out repeating the same ten PR comments every week, seniors review clean, pre-hardened diffs. Whenever a senior catches a genuinely novel domain edge case, Target 90 compiles that senior's personal scar into the shared repository catalog.

That creates a Compounding Review Ratchet: a senior engineer only ever has to teach a lesson once. On the very next git pull, every junior's local Critic enforces—and explains—that lesson automatically.

7. When the Scar Becomes the Spec (noirebox#53)

For months, I thought of our scar registry strictly as defensive armor for our own coding agents. Then Sam LABBE proved it is something much bigger: a portable, cross-platform CVE catalog for autonomous agents.

After reading Part 3.7, Sam took four of our gate-counterfeiting scars—SCAR-PROC-43, SCAR-PROC-45, SCAR-PROC-89, and SCAR-PROC-110, all earned inside our Dart/Flutter workflow—and replayed them as pytest attacks (tests/test_scar_replay.py, noirebox#53) against NoireBox, a Python Ed25519 + SHA-256 flight-recorder built for EU AI Act compliance.

On its very first run, the scar replay caught a live pre-terminal pairing race in NoireBox's reconciler (decision -> FIRST outcome instead of terminal outcome, mirroring SCAR-PROC-110), which Sam fixed in 60 seconds (e9e8d0b). It also exposed an optional spec_hash schema seam (SCAR-PROC-45), closed at the schema hours later (0b888c1) so an LLM-judged receipt without a spec_hash refuses to seal.

As Sam put it in his write-up:

"The fixture didn't just replay your catalog, it caught a live pairing bug on its first day out. That is the difference between a test suite and a breaks-catalog: the catalog finds what the gate's author didn't think to check. The scar becomes the spec."

Why did four scars earned on a Dart monorepo immediately break a Python cryptographic flight recorder? Because agents cheat at the topology layer, not the language layer. Whether your stack is Dart, Python, TypeScript, or Rust, a fatigued LLM exploits the exact same distributed-systems race conditions—stale receipts, premature pairing, self-rubber-stamping, and skipped prerequisites. A well-written scar isn't just a note to self; it is an executable test vector for any agentic system on Earth.

8. Summary & What's Next in Part 6

Moving from paranoid human tele-operation to earned agentic trust isn't about waiting for a mythical "AGI" model that never makes mistakes. It is about building an engineering system that remembers pain and measures the right ledger:

  • Stop coding by majority vote: An unscarred LLM's highest-probability completion is Page 1 tutorial popularity. Compile your 3 AM failures into -∞ vetoes.
  • Optimize T_TWC, not tokens-per-second: Under Boehm's updated $1 : $500 : $25,000 curve, spending fifty cents on a fresh-context Target 40 Critic before git commit is the highest-ROI spend in modern software engineering.
  • Trust the 4-Layer Verification Stack, not syntax squinting: Pair Red-to-Green TDD, the Six-Pillar Critic, Live Socratic Cross-Examination (breaking the cold-crime-scene PR habit), and a Last-Mile Specialist Escape Valve.
  • Let Second-Order Scars and the Teaching Hospital compound: When the Critic catches a blocker on a zero-nudge run—or a senior catches an edge case on a junior's PR—compile it into the shared catalog so the lesson only has to be taught once.
  • Be honest about the ledger: Across 375 tickets, our domain/code repeat regression rate is 0.0%, while 9.87% (37 / 375) of runs still hit process/harness tool-calling reflexes.

Next Up in Part 6: "The Proscriptive Inversion: What You Get to Forget, and Why More Negative Rules Mean You've Lost"

Those 37 harness repeat failures point straight to a deeper architectural law: if you have more rules about what not to do than what to do, you've already lost. In Part 6, we tackle The Straitjacket vs. The Wind Tunnel (why giant 2,000-line .cursorrules and CLAUDE.md files paralyze models), introduce the Unlearning Metric (ΔU)—measuring how much accidental complexity you get to forget—and walk through a real-world architectural case study comparing defensive minefields against clean, generative state machines.

I Built a Programming Language in Bhojpuri from Scratch Using Go

Nobody asked for a Bhojpuri programming language, so I built one.

Meet BiharLang, a dynamically typed, interpreted toy programming language written entirely in Go, with keywords derived from Bhojpuri.

Why I built it

I've always been curious about how programming languages work beneath the syntax we use every day.

I wanted to see how a language parses expressions, applies operator precedence, stores variables and lets functions remember their surrounding scope. Reading about those ideas only got me so far. So I implemented them myself.

Why Bhojpuri? It made the project more fun.

A huge shoutout to the developers behind BhaiLang for the inspiration and to my friends from Bihar who helped me figure out the keywords.

Project structure:

biharlang/
├── cmd/
│   └── bihari/
│       └── main.go                 # CLI entry point (REPL and file runner)
├── lexer/
│   ├── lexer.go                    # Tokenizer implementation
│   └── lexer_test.go               # Lexer unit tests
├── parser/
│   ├── parser.go                   # Pratt parser implementation
│   └── parser_test.go              # Parser unit tests
├── evaluator/
│   ├── evaluator.go                # Tree-walking evaluator
│   ├── evaluator_test.go           # Evaluator unit tests
│   └── environment.go              # Scoped variable environment (closures)
├── ast/
│   └── ast.go                      # Abstract Syntax Tree node definitions
├── object/
│   └── object.go                   # Runtime value types
├── token/
│   └── token.go                    # Token type definitions and keyword lookup
├── repl/
│   └── repl.go                     # Interactive REPL implementation
├── go.mod                          # Go module definition
├── main.bh                         # Example BiharLang script
├── README.md
└── LICENSE

What BiharLang looks like

Here's a simple program:

rakha naam = "Babu"
rakha umar = 25

bol "Ka ho " + naam + "!"
bol umar

Output:

Ka ho Babu!
25

Some of the keywords currently supported are:

BiharLang English equivalent
rakha let / var
bol print
agar if
nata else
jabtak while
kaam function
lauta return
sach true
jhoot false
kuchnahi null

BiharLang also supports functions, recursion and loops. Here's a factorial implementation:

kaam factorial(n) {
    agar (n <= 1) {
        lauta 1
    }

    lauta n * factorial(n - 1)
}

bol factorial(5)

Output:

120

How BiharLang works internally

BiharLang uses a fairly simple interpreter architecture with three major components: a lexer, a parser and an evaluator.

Source Code (.bh)
        |
        v
      Lexer
        |
        v
      Tokens
        |
        v
      Parser
        |
        v
 Abstract Syntax Tree
        |
        v
     Evaluator
        |
        v
   Runtime Values

1. The lexer

The lexer converts raw source code into tokens the parser can understand. Given this BiharLang statement:

rakha x = 10 + 5

It produces tokens that conceptually look like this:

RAKHA
IDENTIFIER(x)
ASSIGN
INTEGER(10)
PLUS
INTEGER(5)
EOF
  • Nothing runs yet. At this stage, the interpreter doesn't evaluate anything
  • The lexer only identifies what each part of the source represents.
  • I implemented it manually in Go, with support for identifiers, keywords, integers, strings and both single-character and multi-character operators.
  • This is also where the Bhojpuri keywords are recognized.

2. The parser

  • Once I had a stream of tokens, I needed to determine how they relate to one another.
  • Why a Pratt parser?
  • It parses expressions according to operator precedence.

Consider this expression:

5 + 3 * 2

Multiplication must happen before addition, so the parser represents the expression as an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST):

       +
      / \
     5   *
        / \
       3   2

The evaluator traverses this tree. The result is 11.

BiharLang currently implements the following precedence levels, from lowest to highest:

  • LOWEST
  • EQUALS
  • LESSGREATER
  • SUM
  • PRODUCT
  • CALL

The Pratt parser also makes it easier to add more operators later.

3. The evaluator

After the parser constructs the AST, the evaluator walks through it recursively. This is where the interpreter runs the program.

For this code:

rakha x = 10 + 5
bol x

The evaluator computes the expression, stores the result in the environment and retrieves it when evaluating the print statement.

Every runtime value in BiharLang implements a common Go interface:

type Object interface {
    Type() ObjectType
    Inspect() string
}

The runtime currently includes integers, strings, booleans, null values, functions, return values and errors.

The language is dynamically typed, so variable types are determined at runtime rather than explicitly declared.

4. Environments and closures

An environment stores variable names and their corresponding runtime values.

Functions create enclosed environments that reference their parent environment, allowing them to access variables from the surrounding lexical scope.

For example:

rakha x = 10

kaam getX() {
    lauta x
}

bol getX()

Output:

10

The function can access x even though it wasn't declared inside the function itself.

Implementing environments gave me a much clearer understanding of lexical scoping and closures than simply using them in other programming languages.

5. The interactive REPL

I also built a REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) so users can run BiharLang interactively without creating a script file:

bh repl

To run a .bh file directly:

bh main.bh

The project includes unit tests for the lexer, parser and evaluator. Run them with:

go test ./... -v

What's next?

BiharLang is still a toy language, and plenty is missing. I'd like to add:

  • Arrays
  • Hash maps
  • Logical operators
  • Break and continue statements
  • Built-in functions
  • User input
  • File I/O

For now, it can execute functions, recursion, loops, expressions and conditionals—which is exactly what I set out to build.

Final thoughts

It isn't meant to replace an existing language. It's a learning project I built for fun, and it's open-source under the MIT license.

GitHub: https://github.com/CoderZ90/BiharLang
Try it live: https://helloadi.vercel.app/projects/biharlang
Linkedin: https://lnkd.in/p/gg6JMejZ
