Most local coding models try to do everything in one trunk: chat, tool calling, chain-of-thought reasoning, and inline autocomplete. Once you shrink a model down to 0.5B-1.5B parameters, mixing chat fine-tuning into cursor autocomplete causes three immediate problems: it leaks markdown fences, forgets when to stop, and feels sluggish while you type.

Over the past few weeks, I have been building The Wisp Family (The Wisp Fieldbook) -- a series of strictly Apache-2.0, non-chat, Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) code-autocomplete specialists trained, distilled, verified, and quantized on a single Apple Silicon Mac (M5 Max, 128 GiB).

Here is where the family stands today, what you can run locally right now, the real blind benchmark receipts from our upcoming Wisp-2.1 release, and four genuinely surprising engineering lessons we uncovered along the way.

Meet The Wisp Family

Every model in the series ships with open Apache-2.0 weights, raw benchmark receipts, and zero chat SFT by design:

  • No. 001 - wisp-coder-110m (Live): A 108M scratch-trained Llama + Multi-Token Prediction research model (live browser demo).
  • No. 002 - Wisp-2-0.8B (Live & Certified): An 854 MiB MLX-8bit hybrid linear-RNN (18 GatedDeltaNet + 6 Full Attention layers) with native EAGLE-3 speculative decoding that hits 27.5 ms warm keystrokes on Apple Silicon. Try it in your browser on the free CPU playground or grab the BF16 weights.
  • No. 003 - Wisp-2.1 (1.5B-Pro + 0.5B-Fast) (In Final Certification): A dual-sibling Pure-FA Qwen2.5-Coder pair distilled on-policy from Apache-2.0 Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. 1.5B-Pro already cleared 11/13 certification gates (every blind quality, roundtrip, decontamination, and 0/1,194 bitwise parity check) while we finalize its upgraded 2-layer EAGLE-3 drafter and 540 MB 0.5B-Fast sibling.

You can browse everything published so far in The Wisp Fieldbook Collection on Hugging Face.

Live Right Now: Wisp-2-0.8B (27.5 ms Keystrokes)

We evaluated Wisp-2-0.8B on Apple M5 Max against our frozen blind Tier-1 suite: 566 holes across 200 files from 30 unseen open-source repositories created strictly after June 1, 2026 (11 languages, matched repo-level FIM headers, identical 8 stop sentinels):

Model (8-bit MLX on M5 Max) PSM Exact Match SPM Exact Match PSM Auto-Stop Warm Keystroke p50 Forced 24-tok p50
Wisp-2-0.8B (EAGLE-3 MTP D=3) 32.86% 30.57% 97.70% (13/566 cap) 27.49 ms 67.03 ms (358 tok/s)
Wisp-2-0.8B (AR, no MTP) -- -- -- 32.81 ms 94.37 ms (1.41x slower)
Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (stock 8-bit) 24.20% 8.13% 66.61% (189/566 cap) 47.98 ms 128.84 ms (1.92x slower)
Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B (stock 8-bit) 14.66% 3.18% 42.05% (328/566 cap) 72.75 ms 73.22 ms
Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base (raw start) 0.53% (62x lift) -- 89.22% -- --

The biggest surprise in that table wasn't parameter count -- it was autonomous stopping. Under identical headers and stop tokens, stock Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B slammed into the 256-token cap on 328/566 holes (16x median length ratio), and stock 1.5B hit the cap on 189/566 (3x median length). Wisp-2-0.8B stopped cleanly on 97.70% of holes with a 1.0x ideal length ratio and 0% markdown fence leaks.

Where Wisp-2-0.8B Hit a Wall (and Why We Didn't Hide It)

On standalone executable algorithms from scratch (Tier-2A, 80 tasks across 8 compilers/runtimes in a macOS Seatbelt sandbox), Wisp-2-0.8B improved 4.3x over its raw base (37.5% vs 8.8%), but still trailed 5.5T-token code-pretrained Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (76.25%), and sat at 3.33% (8/240) on real-repo executable bodies (Tier-2B).

When we tried pushing a second iteration on the 0.8B hybrid trunk, it hit 20.85 ms warm keystrokes and passed 11/13 gates -- yet flatlined at 37.5% Tier-2A (4.58% Tier-2B). Instead of shipping a half-win, we executed an honest auto-revert and pivoted No. 003 (Wisp-2.1) to a dual-sibling Pure-FA Qwen2.5-Coder architecture distilled directly from Apache-2.0 Qwen2.5-Coder-32B.

Inside Wisp-2.1 (In Final Certification Now)

Switching to Pure-FA Qwen2.5-Coder (1.5B-Pro at 1.53 GB + 0.5B-Fast at 540 MB) unlocked two huge advantages:

  1. Exact same-tokenizer soft-logit On-Policy Distillation (GKD-OPD) from Apache-2.0 Qwen2.5-Coder-32B (:151936 exact logit alignment, sparse K=64 covering 99.84% probability mass in Phase 1 + live 32B on-policy rollouts in Phase 2).
  2. O(1) KV-cache rollback on speculative draft rejections with zero linear-RNN state snapshot overhead.

Here are the actual blind Stage-11 numbers already recorded on Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro's frozen 8-bit trunk across all four frozen benchmarks (every single blind quality, roundtrip, decontamination, and 0/1,194 bitwise speculative parity gate passed):

Benchmark (Frozen Blind & Sandboxed Suites) Wisp-2-0.8B (No. 002) Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (stock 8-bit) Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro (Frozen Trunk, 8-bit)
Tier-1 Blind EM (n=566, post-June-2026 repos) 31.80% (mixed) 24.20% PSM / 8.13% SPM 37.99% (35.34% PSM / 40.64% SPM)
Tier-1 Multi-Line EditSim / AST (n=240, 10 langs) 0.2310 / 73.3% -- 0.3425 (+11.2 pp) / 82.5% AST
Tier-2A Executable Algorithms (n=80, 8 langs) 37.50% (30/80) 76.25% (61/80) 90.00% (72/80) (100% C, C++, Go, Swift)
Tier-2B Blind Executable Repos (n=240, 8 langs) 3.33% (8/240) 7.92% (19/240) 12.50% (30/240) (3.75x Wisp-2, +58% vs stock)
DEV Exec128_v2 (vs JetBrains Mellum-4B: 35/128) -- -- 50.0% (64/128)

Full transparency on why it isn't public yet: On our first full Stage-11 run, Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro passed 11/13 gates and held strictly on the long-context (1,791-token) warm speculative latency bar (34.13 ms vs 31.95 ms AR with a 1-layer EAGLE-3 drafter). Because EAGLE-3 speculative decoding is 100% lossless (0/1,194 mismatches against greedy AR), we are training an upgraded 2-layer Pre-Norm EAGLE-3 drafter right now to push warm latency well under our <= 32 ms / >= 1.25x AR bar -- keeping every quality number above bitwise identical -- and then finishing its 540 MB Wisp-2.1-0.5B-Fast sibling before public release.

Four Counterintuitive Engineering Lessons From Training on One Mac

1. FP32-Scale 8-Bit Quantization Was Both Cleaner and Faster Than FP16

During Wisp-2's 1,000-round speculative parity audit, standard FP16-scale 8-bit quantization produced 4 subtle token tie flips from 1-ULP rounding on the FP16 logit grid (0.015625). Promoting only the quantization scales and GDN recurrence states to FP32 while keeping weights packed in 8-bit (854.1 MiB, group_size=64) eliminated every tie (0/1,000 drift, 1.000000 cosine vs stock mlx_lm.load()), lifted blind EM, and actually ran slightly faster than FP16.

2. Zero-Step Uniform 8-Bit PTQ Beat Every 8-Bit QAT Run We Tried

Before running Stage-11 on Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro, we ran a 7-candidate controlled DEV compression factorial on our 32B-distilled BF16 trunk (65/128 Exec128_v2, 73/80 Tier-2A). To our surprise, zero-step uniform 8-bit PTQ (group_size=64, zero gradient steps) beat or tied every 8-bit QAT run:

  • 0-step uniform 8-bit PTQ: 64/128 Exec128_v2, 72/80 Tier-2A, 5.83% ML600 severe truncation, 0.999776 logit cosine, and only 1/3,414 (0.029%) EOS flips vs BF16.
  • Why QAT drifted earlier: An off-by-one bug in our KL anchor covered code tokens 0..M-1 and left the terminal EOS position (t = M) unanchored against the parent while anti-echo penalties pushed EOS logits upward. Anchoring terminal EOS cut QAT truncations nearly in half (60 -> 38/600) -- and proved zero-step PTQ (35/600) had no quantization damage left to heal.

Takeaway: Always run the zero-step PTQ control before spending GPU hours trying to heal quantization damage that isn't there.

3. Qwen2.5 Massive-Activation Sink Channels Break Naive EAGLE-3

Naive EAGLE-3 stalled on Qwen2.5-Coder because Qwen2.5 carries extreme activation-sink channels (133.1 on 0.5B, 4,096.0 on 1.5B) that get crushed up to 721:1 after the final RMSNorm. Switching to pre-final-norm 3-tap fusion (L2, L13, L27_pre), pre-norm recurrent state feedback (applying self.norm strictly on the logit branch), downstream RMSNorm warm-starting, Global Best-Fit Decreasing block packing (99.84% occupancy), and pure HASS_KL(K=32) unlocked lossless speculative drafting on Apple Silicon MLX.

4. Know What to Kill on the Receipts

Not every popular technique wins at sub-2B scale:

  • Mixed 4-bit at 0.8B: Lost -1.6 to -2.3 pp exact match and ran slower (27.8 ms vs 27.5 ms) because dequantization overhead outweighed bandwidth savings. Withheld.
  • W4-MLP at 1.5B: Degraded Python PSM and multi-line EditSim with negligible speed gain under speculative verify shapes on M5 Max. Retired.
  • Single-turn RLVR (Dr.GRPO-FIM): Even with an Ed25519-signed Bonferroni-252 sandbox verifier recording 0/2,016 false positives and 0/240 false negatives across 8 languages, single-turn RLVR dropped Exec128_v2 from 65/128 to 60/128. We closed RLVR cleanly instead of reward-hacking past the numbers.

Run Wisp-2-0.8B Locally on Mac in 60 Seconds

You don't need our training repo to run Wisp locally. The MLX-8bit Hugging Face repo bundles a self-contained, zero-dependency wisp_runtime/ package exposing a local OpenAI-compatible & /v1/fim/completions server (Continue.dev and Zed ready, loopback-only by default):

hf download philipjohnbasile/Wisp-2-0.8B-MLX-8bit --local-dir ./Wisp-2-0.8B-MLX-8bit
cd ./Wisp-2-0.8B-MLX-8bit
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Quick single-completion smoke test
python -m wisp_runtime.serve --bundle-dir . --demo

# Start the local 27.5 ms autocomplete server
python -m wisp_runtime.serve --bundle-dir . --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8091

Or test it right now without installing anything on the Wisp-2 Live CPU Playground.

What's Next

  1. Finishing Wisp-2.1 (1.5B-Pro + 0.5B-Fast): Wrapping up the 2-layer EAGLE-3 drafter for 1.5B-Pro, running the full 13-gate Stage-11 certification for both siblings, and shipping a dual-sibling Hugging Face Space + standalone wisp_runtime/ packages.
  2. Researching Wisp-3.0: A dual-brother local coding architecture on Apple Silicon -- keeping a sub-25 ms Wisp cursor reflex model co-resident in unified memory alongside a strictly permissive (MIT / Apache-2.0) deep repair sibling with a deterministic evidence-selection memory layer.

If you're experimenting with MLX, speculative decoding, hybrid SSM/attention architectures, or small coding models on Apple Silicon, I'd love to hear your thoughts or benchmark numbers on M1-M5 Macs!

articles.title: mmap, fsync, and WALs: Low-Level Lessons That Make System Design Click
articles.description: When I started building systems, my primary motivation was to understand what happens underneath the...
articles.body_html:
When I started building systems, my primary motivation was to understand what happens underneath the abstractions we use every day.

How does a database actually persist data? Why do storage engines use different indexing structures? How does the operating system manage file-backed memory? Why does adding more threads sometimes make an application slower rather than faster?

Initially, these seemed like isolated engineering problems. But as I worked on storage engines, distributed search systems, and concurrent applications, I started noticing something interesting.

The principles governing low-level systems are often the same principles behind high-level system design.

Understanding them from the ground up made several architectural decisions that previously seemed arbitrary feel almost intuitive.

Here are some of the connections I discovered along the way.

1. mmap vs pread + LRU: Choosing How Data Enters Memory

One of the interesting decisions I encountered while building storage systems was choosing between memory-mapped files and explicit file reads.

Both approaches allow applications to access data stored on disk, but they offer fundamentally different models.

With mmap, a file is mapped into a process's virtual address space. Instead of explicitly reading blocks into application-managed buffers, the application accesses the mapped region as if it were memory. The operating system handles page loading through page faults and the page cache.

This is particularly useful when data is already stored in a representation that can be consumed directly.

I encountered this while building Turbo Query, a distributed hybrid search engine combining BM25 with semantic reranking using MiniLM embeddings.

Each document has an associated 384-dimensional embedding. These vectors are stored as contiguous floating-point arrays in a binary file.

During a search, BM25 first retrieves a relatively small set of candidate documents. Instead of loading the entire vector dataset into application memory, I use mmap to access the corresponding vectors directly and calculate cosine similarity for semantic reranking.

This makes memory-mapped access a natural fit for the workload.

The data is already in the representation required by the computation. There is no need to deserialize the entire vector store into another in-memory structure.

mmap has costs too, which the CIDR 2022 paper "Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your DBMS?" (Crotty, Leis, Pavlo) covers well. A read can silently stall while the operating system fetches data from disk, and my code can't see when that happens. The OS also decides what stays in memory, not me. If a read fails, the program can crash instead of getting an error it can handle. And since the file is just raw bytes, I have to be careful that they are interpreted as numbers correctly. I accepted these costs for Turbo Query because the vectors are read-only, fixed-size, and already in the layout the similarity computation needs.

On the other hand, pread provides explicit control over reading data into application-managed buffers at specified file offsets.

Combined with an LRU cache, this becomes useful when the application needs more control over what gets loaded, retained, evicted, and processed.

In BedrockDB, an LSM-tree-based storage engine, records are persisted in an encoded representation. Accessing a record involves reading the relevant data from disk, decoding it, and reconstructing its in-memory representation before it can be consumed.

An explicit pread + LRU approach provides greater control over block reads, buffer management, and caching. Frequently accessed blocks can remain in memory, avoiding repeated disk reads.

The distinction isn't that one approach is universally faster than the other.

It depends on the data representation, access pattern, memory constraints, and processing requirements.

If data can be consumed directly in its stored representation, mmap can be a natural choice. If access requires explicit loading, transformation, and buffer management, pread + LRU can offer greater control.

2. Why More Parallelism Can Sometimes Hurt Performance

One of the most interesting lessons from building Turbo Query came from optimizing concurrency.

The initial assumption was straightforward: more concurrent workers should translate into higher throughput.

But that isn't necessarily true.

Parallelism is particularly effective when workloads are compute-bound. If multiple independent tasks require substantial CPU computation, distributing them across available cores can improve throughput. Think of a GPU. Its architecture is designed to execute thousands of operations concurrently, making it particularly effective for highly parallel computational workloads such as matrix multiplication, image processing, and neural network inference.

However, memory-bound workloads behave differently.

Consider what happens when multiple workers continuously access large regions of memory.

Eventually, the bottleneck might not be CPU availability. It might be memory bandwidth, cache misses, or contention within the memory subsystem.

Adding more workers can increase competition for shared resources instead of improving useful work completed per second.

I encountered this while working on Turbo Query.

The search engine uses Bleve for BM25 retrieval and memory-mapped vector storage for semantic reranking.

During performance testing, I observed significant latency fluctuations under unrestricted concurrency. Bleve latency varied from approximately 4 ms to 400 ms.

Instead of continuing to increase concurrency, I introduced bounded parallelism using a semaphore initialized with four permits.

This limited the number of concurrent workers accessing the workload.

The observed latency subsequently stabilized around 3–5 ms.

The important realization was that unrestricted concurrency was introducing more contention than useful parallelism.

Several factors can contribute to this behaviour:

  • Increased context switching.
  • Cache and TLB pressure.
  • Memory-system contention.
  • Competition for shared resources.
  • Additional synchronization overhead.

The solution wasn't to maximize the number of concurrent operations. It was to find a concurrency level that allowed the system to operate efficiently.

This is particularly important for memory-bound workloads, where additional CPU workers cannot necessarily increase the rate at which data is supplied from memory.

There is another interesting connection here.

This is the same reasoning behind bounded worker pools, connection pools, and backpressure mechanisms in distributed systems.

We don't want an application to accept unlimited work simply because it can create more goroutines or threads.

We want to control how much work enters the system at a time.

Concurrency is a resource that needs to be managed, not a number that should always be maximized.

3. fsync Batching: Amortizing Expensive Operations

Another interesting lesson came from understanding durable writes.

Writing data to a file and ensuring that it has reached persistent storage are two different things.

An fsync operation requests synchronization of modified file data and relevant metadata with the underlying storage device.

However, synchronization operations can be expensive.

Consider a workload where every individual write is followed by an fsync.

If we perform 100 writes, we might end up paying the synchronization cost 100 times.

An alternative is to batch multiple writes and synchronize them together.

Instead of:

Write → fsync

Write → fsync

Write → fsync

We can do:

Write → Write → Write → fsync

This is closely related to group commit in database systems.

The underlying idea is simple: amortize the cost of an expensive operation across multiple units of useful work.

Of course, batching introduces a trade-off. Individual writes may have to wait longer before becoming durable, and the system must account for the consequences of a crash before synchronization completes.

But the throughput improvement can be substantial.

This principle extends far beyond storage systems.

We see similar ideas in:

  • Batch database inserts.
  • Bulk API operations.
  • Message batching.
  • Network packet aggregation.
  • Distributed data processing.

Sometimes, optimizing a system isn't about making an individual operation cheaper. It is about making each expensive operation accomplish more work.

4. LSM Trees vs B-Trees: Architecture Follows Workload

Building and understanding storage engines also changed how I think about database selection.

A common oversimplification is that B-trees belong to SQL databases and LSM trees belong to NoSQL databases.

The actual distinction is much more interesting.

B-trees and LSM trees represent different approaches to organizing persistent data.

B-trees support efficient lookups and updates through a page-oriented indexing structure. They are widely used in databases that need balanced read and write performance.

LSM trees optimize write paths by accumulating updates in memory and flushing them to disk as sorted structures. These structures are subsequently merged through compaction.

This makes LSM-based storage engines particularly attractive for write-intensive workloads.

However, they introduce trade-offs involving read amplification, write amplification, and compaction overhead.

The important distinction is the workload, not whether the database exposes SQL or NoSQL interfaces.

Modern NoSQL databases can also provide strong consistency guarantees. Consistency is a property of the database's architecture and configuration, not simply its query language.

Understanding B-trees and LSM trees taught me to evaluate databases based on their underlying storage characteristics rather than their labels.

5. Sequential Writes vs In-Place Writes

This connects directly to the previous section.

Traditional in-place update strategies modify existing data structures on disk. Depending on the storage engine, this can involve random I/O and additional coordination.

LSM-based systems take a different approach.

Instead of repeatedly modifying existing disk structures, they favor sequential writes to new storage files, followed by background compaction.

Why is this useful?

Sequential I/O generally provides more predictable and efficient storage access patterns than scattered random writes, particularly on traditional storage devices.

It also simplifies certain aspects of write-path design.

But this doesn't mean sequential writes are universally superior. Compaction introduces additional I/O, and the system must manage multiple versions of data until they are merged.

The broader lesson is that storage architecture is fundamentally about managing the cost of moving data between memory and persistent storage.

Once you understand that, many database design decisions become easier to reason about.

6. From WAL to Kafka: Recognizing the Same Abstraction

Perhaps the most interesting connection I made was between implementing a Write-Ahead Log in BedrockDB and understanding Kafka.

A Write-Ahead Log, or WAL, is a mechanism used by storage engines to ensure recoverability.

Before modifying the primary in-memory or on-disk representation of data, changes are recorded in a sequential log.

A simplified workflow looks like this:

  1. Receive a write request.
  2. Append the operation to the WAL.
  3. Ensure the required durability guarantees are met.
  4. Apply the change to the in-memory data structure.
  5. Recover the state by replaying the log after a failure, if necessary.

Having implemented the WAL in BedrockDB, I began recognizing the same underlying abstraction when I studied Kafka: the append-only log.

Kafka.

Kafka organizes messages into append-only, partitioned logs. Producers append records, consumers read them sequentially, and the system maintains offsets to track consumption.

Kafka is not simply a database WAL. Their responsibilities, retention models, and recovery semantics differ.

However, understanding the WAL made Kafka's underlying storage abstraction much easier to understand.

The common idea is the append-only log.

Instead of treating updates as isolated modifications, represent changes as an ordered sequence of records.

This is a powerful abstraction that appears in databases, event sourcing, distributed logs, and recovery systems.

One concept learned while building a storage engine suddenly became useful for understanding a completely different system.

7. Why Systems Knowledge Makes System Design More Intuitive

This is probably the biggest takeaway from building these systems.

We often approach system design as a collection of architectural patterns.

Caching, sharding, replication, message queues, load balancing, database selection, and horizontal scaling.

We learn when to use Redis, when to introduce Kafka, when to partition a database, and when to add more application instances.

But understanding the underlying systems changes the way we approach these decisions.

Consider a few examples:

Low-level systems concept High-level system design connection
mmap and page cache OS-managed caching & zero-copy reads
pread + LRU Explicit buffer management and caching
Bounded parallelism Worker pools and backpressure
Memory bandwidth contention Concurrency and resource bottlenecks
fsync batching Batch processing and group commit
LSM trees Write-optimized storage engines
B-trees Efficient indexing and read-heavy workloads
Sequential writes Append-only storage architectures
Write-Ahead Log Kafka's append-only log abstraction

These aren't merely superficial similarities.

They are manifestations of recurring engineering principles.

When you understand why sequential writes are useful, you have a better foundation for understanding append-only architectures.

When you understand why LRU caching works, Redis eviction policies become easier to reason about.

When you understand why fsync batching improves throughput, database group commit and bulk processing make more sense.

When you understand memory bandwidth limitations, you become more careful about introducing parallelism into a workload.

The abstractions change, but many of the underlying constraints remain.

There are, of course, additional complexities at higher levels. Distributed systems introduce network partitions, replication, consensus, failure recovery, and consistency challenges that cannot be reduced to operating-system concepts.

But having a foundation in systems programming makes reasoning about these architectures considerably easier.

Closing Thoughts

I initially started building systems to understand how things worked underneath the abstractions.

What I didn't expect was how much that experience would change the way I understood software architecture.

Building a storage engine taught me about WALs. Understanding WALs helped me understand Kafka. Working with memory-mapped files taught me about the operating system's memory management. Implementing LRU caching helped me reason about application-level caching. Optimizing Turbo Query taught me that unrestricted parallelism can sometimes hurt performance rather than improve it.

These connections gradually changed my approach to engineering.

I no longer see system design as memorizing a collection of architectural patterns and knowing when to apply them.

I see it as understanding constraints, identifying bottlenecks, evaluating trade-offs, and choosing an architecture that fits the workload.

The more I learned about how systems work underneath, the more naturally I began to understand how to design them at a higher level.

And perhaps that is one of the most valuable things about building systems from the ground up: you don't just learn how to implement them. You develop an intuition for why they are designed the way they are.

articles.title: Your Linux Rice Is a Screensaver With Extra Steps
articles.description: Stop tuning border radii for a screenshot. Wire your desktop so it tells you the truth about your...
articles.body_html:
Stop tuning border radii for a screenshot. Wire your desktop so it tells you the truth about your machine.

Somewhere tonight a man is on his third evening of matching the corner radius of his notification daemon to the padding of his terminal. His laptop has had a failed systemd unit since August and a database listening on every interface since a tutorial he followed in the spring.

He will post the screenshot. It will do numbers. The machine underneath will keep lying to him in a perfectly harmonized palette.

The Screenshot Is the Product, and That's the Problem

Ricing culture optimizes for a still frame. The wallpaper, the gaps, the transparent terminal with neofetch running in it: all of it is built to look good for the half second a stranger spends scrolling past. Clone ten Hyprland dotfile repos and you will find ten gorgeous bars that report the same four facts: time, battery, volume, workspace. Your phone already knows all four.

A desktop is an instrument panel. Every pixel you keep on screen permanently should either stay quiet or tell you something true that you would otherwise miss. Pilots don't ask whether the altimeter matches the seat fabric.

I ship a VHS-grain theme suite for KDE Plasma 6 called nightfeed, so I have no quarrel with pretty. Scanlines, tape noise, cobalt black, one palette generating everything from the boot splash to the terminal colors. It installs in one line and backs up your configs first:

$ bash ~/nightfeed/apply.sh            # install + switch, backs up configs to backup/
$ bash ~/nightfeed/apply.sh --revert   # restore the last backup

Paint is fine. Paint is the last coat. The order matters, and most rices get it backwards: months on the surface, zero minutes on the wiring.

Three Questions Your Bar Should Answer

Forget the weather widget. A useful bar answers questions you would never think to ask until the answer hurts.

What on this machine is listening to the network right now? Every dev box accumulates listeners. A Jupyter server, a Vite dev server someone started with --host, a Postgres container that published its port to 0.0.0.0 because Docker does that by default. You don't notice until the coffee shop Wi-Fi notices for you.

What broke while I wasn't looking? systemd will happily let a backup timer fail for three months. It logs the failure. Nobody reads the log.

Does my config match what's in git? If your dotfiles repo is dirty, your machine is a snowflake again, and the next fresh install will cost you a weekend.

Each answer is a ten-line shell script that prints one line of JSON. Waybar's custom module reads exactly that: a text field for the bar, a tooltip for the hover, and a class you can style. Here's the listener check:

#!/bin/sh
# ~/.config/waybar/scripts/listen.sh
# TCP listeners that are NOT bound to loopback
# -H no header, -t tcp, -l listening, -n numeric, -p owning process
lines=$(ss -Htlnp | awk '$4 !~ /^(127\.|\[::1\]|\[::ffff:127\.)/')
n=$(printf '%s' "$lines" | grep -c .)
tip=$(printf '%s\n' "$lines" | awk '{print $4, $6}')
class=quiet
[ "$n" -gt 0 ] && class=exposed
jq -nc --arg text "ears $n" --arg tooltip "$tip" --arg class "$class" \
  '{text: $text, tooltip: $tooltip, class: $class}'

Run it with a throwaway server open and you get something like this:

$ python3 -m http.server 18080 --bind 0.0.0.0 &
$ sh ~/.config/waybar/scripts/listen.sh
{"text":"ears 1","tooltip":"0.0.0.0:18080 users:((\"python3\",pid=618,fd=3))","class":"exposed"}

One gotcha. Without root, ss -p only shows the owning process for sockets your user owns. System daemons show up as a bare address and port. That's enough to make you look; sudo ss -tlnp finishes the job.

Failed units, system and user, in one count:

#!/bin/sh
# ~/.config/waybar/scripts/units.sh
failed=$( { systemctl --failed --no-legend --plain
            systemctl --user --failed --no-legend --plain; } 2>/dev/null |
          awk '{print $1}' | grep . )
n=$(printf '%s' "$failed" | grep -c .)
class=ok
[ "$n" -gt 0 ] && class=broken
jq -nc --arg text "fail $n" --arg tooltip "$failed" --arg class "$class" \
  '{text: $text, tooltip: $tooltip, class: $class}'

And drift between your machine and your dotfiles repo, counting uncommitted changes and commits you never pushed:

#!/bin/sh
# ~/.config/waybar/scripts/dotfiles.sh
repo="$HOME/dotfiles"
dirty=$(git -C "$repo" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null | grep -c .)
ahead=$(git -C "$repo" rev-list --count '@{u}..HEAD' 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
class=clean
[ "$dirty" -gt 0 ] || [ "$ahead" -gt 0 ] && class=drift
jq -nc --arg text "dots ${dirty}/${ahead}" \
  --arg tooltip "$dirty uncommitted, $ahead unpushed in $repo" \
  --arg class "$class" '{text: $text, tooltip: $tooltip, class: $class}'

Once you see the pattern (run a command, count the bad lines, emit JSON) you'll want twenty more of these. The disk that's 94% full. The SMART counter that started climbing. The VPN that silently dropped. If you'd rather start from a pile of working scripts than write each one from scratch, The Bash Necromancer ($33) is 150 Bash scripts for monitoring, file operations, automation and system administration, written with reviewable inputs and outputs. Most of the monitoring ones become a bar module by swapping their last line for the jq call above.

Wiring Them Into Waybar

The module config is boring on purpose. Each entry points at a script, declares JSON output, and sets a polling interval:

// ~/.config/waybar/config.jsonc (inside your top-level object)
"modules-right": ["custom/listen", "custom/units", "custom/dotfiles", "clock"],

"custom/listen": {
  "exec": "~/.config/waybar/scripts/listen.sh",
  "return-type": "json",
  "interval": 15,
  "on-click": "foot -e sh -c 'sudo ss -tlnp; read _'"
},
"custom/units": {
  "exec": "~/.config/waybar/scripts/units.sh",
  "return-type": "json",
  "interval": 60,
  "on-click": "foot -e sh -c 'systemctl --failed; read _'"
},
"custom/dotfiles": {
  "exec": "~/.config/waybar/scripts/dotfiles.sh",
  "return-type": "json",
  "interval": 300,
  "signal": 9
}

Swap foot for whatever terminal you run. Then the only CSS that matters: quiet when things are fine, loud when they aren't. Waybar turns custom/listen into the id #custom-listen, and your class value lands on it.

/* ~/.config/waybar/style.css */
#custom-listen.quiet,
#custom-units.ok,
#custom-dotfiles.clean { opacity: 0.35; }

#custom-listen.exposed,
#custom-units.broken { color: #ff5f5f; }

#custom-dotfiles.drift { color: #e0af68; }

A healthy machine fades into the bar. A sick one turns red. That's the whole design system, and it beats any gradient you'll ever tune.

The signal line on the dotfiles module is the nice trick. Waybar refreshes a module early when it receives SIGRTMIN plus that number, so a git hook can update the bar the instant you commit instead of waiting five minutes:

#!/bin/sh
# ~/dotfiles/.git/hooks/post-commit  (chmod +x it)
pkill -RTMIN+9 waybar

Commit, and the amber goes grey before your hand leaves the keyboard. Small feedback loops are how habits get built.

One Key That Ends the Session

The other thing a real desktop needs is a panic button: one chord that kills the mic, stops whatever is playing, and locks the screen, for when someone walks up behind you or you walk away from the table:

#!/bin/sh
# ~/.local/bin/lockdown
wpctl set-mute @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SOURCE@ 1   # mic off at the PipeWire level
playerctl pause 2>/dev/null               # stop media if anything is playing
swaylock -f -c 000000                     # fork, lock, solid black

Bind it in Sway:

bindsym $mod+Escape exec ~/.local/bin/lockdown

Or in Hyprland:

bind = $mainMod, Escape, exec, ~/.local/bin/lockdown

Muting at the PipeWire source means the call app doesn't get a vote. That's the right default for a key you press in a hurry.

If It Isn't Reproducible, It Isn't Yours

Everything above lives in four small files and two config blocks. Put them in the dotfiles repo the third module is watching, and your next machine gets the instrument panel for free. Leave them scattered in ~/.config and you'll rebuild them from memory, badly, at 2 AM, after a dead SSD.

This is where most rices quietly fail. They were assembled by hand over a year of copy-paste, and nobody, including the owner, can say what's load-bearing. The move that fixes it is boring: one repo, one install path, ideally a declarative system underneath so the machine itself is described in text. If you want the whole road mapped, the Linux Desktop Operator Pack ($39) is eleven guides covering an Arch install path, the move to NixOS and flakes, Sway layouts, EWW widgets and dashboards, KDE and SDDM theming, dotfiles and reproducible builds. It's the right next step if your current setup works but you couldn't rebuild it on a fresh drive by Sunday.

Pick the one module that would have embarrassed you most last month. Wire that one tonight. Leave the corner radius alone until the bar has something to say.

articles.title: Is your cheapest AI task running on your most expensive model?
articles.description: Five helper agents read through my repos one day in August. They did a lovely job. They read every...
articles.body_html:
Five helper agents read through my repos one day in August. They did a lovely job. They read every file they were pointed at, counted what they were asked to count and wrote tidy summaries.

Together they used about 400,000 tokens, every one of them at the price of my most expensive model. The job was reading. A model a third of the price does reading just as well.

Nobody had chosen that. That was the bug.

Scene one: the report that said 9 per cent

Three days earlier, our cost report had shown a reassuring number: only 9 per cent of the work ran on the expensive model. The rest went to cheaper ones, the way it's supposed to: the big model plans, smaller models do the work.

Then I read how the report counted. It only counted the helpers. The main session, the one that plans, reads CI logs, merges and talks to me for a hundred turns with an ever-growing context, wasn't in any number at all. The 9 per cent wasn't a cost figure. It was a statistic about who got delegated to.

We fixed the counting and moved the main session to a model at half the price. Problem solved, I thought.

Scene two: the helpers nobody configured

Three days after that came the five readers.

Our task workers had their model pinned per tier: small tasks to the smallest model, harder ones one step up. But the quick "go and read this for me" helpers, the inventories and the "find out how X works" jobs, had no model written down anywhere. So they used whatever the main session was running. That day, the main session was running the most expensive model.

So five readers ran at architect prices, doing work that has nothing to do with architecture.

The list prices at the time, per million tokens in and out:

The reading helpers belonged on the second rung. They ran on the top one, at more than three times the price per token, for identical output.

The one line

The fix, the next night at 01:19, was a file with one line that mattered (shortened here):

---
name: scout
description: "Read-only research agent. Inventories, codebase questions."
model: sonnet
---

Every reading job now goes through that agent type. And the rule behind it is short: no helper silently inherits the session's model. Whoever starts one names the model.

A line that people have to remember is a line that gets forgotten again. So the same night we added a check: a small tool compares the routing table (which role gets which model) with the agent files, and reports any mismatch as drift. model: inherit counts as drift too. The expensive model is allowed in exactly three roles: the one architecture run, audits, and the last escalation step. Anywhere else it needs a written reason in the log.

In the next batch of tasks, four ran on the mid-tier model, one on the smallest, and the expensive model only did the planning and coordination.

The class of bug

This isn't really about AI models. It's about defaults:

A role without a pinned setting falls back to the most expensive thing that happens to be running.

You'll find the same shape in a CI job that never names its runner size, a container without resource limits sitting next to a hungry neighbour, or a background job that inherits the credentials of whoever started it. Nobody picks the expensive option. It's just what's left when nothing was picked.

It stays invisible for the same reason as my 9 per cent: the report counts what is easy to count, and inherited settings are exactly what nobody counts.

The two-minute check

If you use agent definitions, list which model each one runs on:

for f in .claude/agents/*.md; do
  m=$(grep -m1 '^model:' "$f" | awk '{print $2}')
  echo "${m:-MISSING}  $f"
done | sort

Every MISSING or inherit is a helper whose price depends on what your main session happens to be doing. Then answer two more questions:

  1. Where do you start helpers without an agent type at all? Ad-hoc "go and research this" helpers are the usual suspects.
  2. Does your cost number include the main session? If it only counts helpers, it's a delegation statistic, not a bill.

None of this needs a new tool. It needs one line per role, and one check that tells you when a role lost its line.

Next in this series: the day my AI almost made me shut down half our databases, because of one example in the code.

Which of your helpers is quietly running on your most expensive setting?

I build cachly. It keeps what you explain to your AI: your rules, your decisions and the bugs you already solved. Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and the others read it in every session, for you alone or for your whole team, and every lesson carries the name of whoever learned it.

Try it, in increasing order of commitment:

  • 30 seconds, no account: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest demo in any git repo. It reads your log locally and prints what an assistant would already know about the project. After npx fetches the package, the command makes no network calls.
  • Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add cachly-dev/cachly-mcp, then /plugin install cachly-brain@cachly.
  • 5 minutes, free tier: npx @cachly-dev/mcp-server@latest autopilot writes the MCP configuration for whichever assistant you use.
  • Or from the web: cachly.dev · free tier, servers in Germany.

On Product Hunt from 1 December: cachly on Product Hunt. Follow it there if you want a note on launch day.

articles.description: Put a fake server on your own LAN. Anything that touches it is telling on itself.  There is a box on...
articles.body_html:
Put a fake server on your own LAN. Anything that touches it is telling on itself.

There is a box on my network that does nothing. It has a hostname that sounds like a backup NAS, six open ports that look like a tired Ubuntu server, and no legitimate reason for any device in the house to ever speak to it.

So when something does, my phone buzzes.

That's the entire trick, and it's older than most of the security industry. Real services have real traffic, which means real noise to dig through. A decoy has no traffic at all. Its baseline is zero, and zero is the easiest number in the world to alert on.

Why a Decoy Beats Another Dashboard

Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 put the global median dwell time at 14 days: two weeks between an intruder getting in and anyone noticing. Organizations that caught it themselves did so in about 9 days. The ones who heard about it from someone else waited a median of 25. And in the intrusions where initial access got handed off to a second crew, the median handoff took 22 seconds.

Those are corporate numbers with corporate budgets. Your house has a router, a dozen smart plugs from brands that stopped shipping firmware in 2023, a kid's gaming laptop, and you. Nobody is reading your logs. Nobody is going to call you in 25 days.

Whatever lands on a home network first does what intruders always do: it looks around. It sweeps the subnet, knocks on SSH, tries the file shares. A decoy turns that first look into a push notification. You stop needing to win the detection game in general. You only need to be the thing they touch.

The Bait Box

Any always-on Linux machine works. An old laptop with the lid closed is fine. I like a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B [AFFILIATE: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B] on Ethernet because it draws a few watts and disappears behind the router.

Two setup details make the trap believable:

  1. A reserved IP in your router's DHCP settings, so the address never moves and your alerts stay readable.
  2. A boring, tempting hostname. Something like ds220-backup reads as a Synology box full of family photos and tax PDFs. That's what someone poking around a home network wants.

If you run a real SSH server on this machine, move it off port 22 first, because the trap needs that port. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config set Port 2222, restart sshd, and confirm you can still log in on 2222 before you go further. Locking yourself out of your own honeypot is a rite of passage you can skip.

Option One: OpenCanary in Ten Minutes

Thinkst, the company behind the commercial Canary appliances, publishes an open-source version called OpenCanary. It needs Python 3.10 or newer. On Ubuntu or Raspberry Pi OS:

$ sudo apt-get install python3-dev python3-pip python3-virtualenv python3-venv python3-scapy libssl-dev libpcap-dev
$ virtualenv env/
$ . env/bin/activate
$ pip install opencanary
$ sudo env/bin/opencanaryd --copyconfig

That last command writes a JSON config to /etc/opencanaryd/opencanary.conf. Open it, set "device.node_id" to something unique, and flip the services you want from false to true: "ssh.enabled", "telnet.enabled", "http.enabled", plus "portscan.enabled" if you want scan detection (Linux only, since it manipulates iptables). The sample config already logs to /var/tmp/opencanary.log as one JSON object per line.

Start it and let it drop root once the ports are bound:

$ . env/bin/activate
$ opencanaryd --start --uid=nobody --gid=nogroup

OpenCanary is the right call if you want breadth: it speaks enough of many protocols to keep a curious visitor engaged, and it can push alerts through its own logging handlers. The cost is a stack of dependencies you didn't write, sitting on a box you're trusting to tell you the truth.

Option Two: A Tripwire You Can Read in One Sitting

I wanted something I could audit end to end, so I wrote a small one. Standard library only. It opens six ports, plays a convincing banner on the ones where a banner is expected, records who connected and the first thing they said, and sends a push through ntfy. It refuses to keep passwords: on the fake web login it stores the request line and whether credentials were attempted, never the credentials themselves.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""tripwire: fake services on a box nothing should ever touch."""
import asyncio
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone

PORTS = {
    21: b"220 (vsFTPd 3.0.5)\r\n",
    22: b"SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13.5\r\n",
    23: b"\r\nDS220 login: ",
    80: None,    # wait for the request, answer with a login prompt
    445: None,   # say nothing, just listen
    3389: None,
}
LOG = os.environ.get("TRIPWIRE_LOG", "/var/lib/tripwire/hits.jsonl")
NTFY = os.environ.get("TRIPWIRE_NTFY")  # https://ntfy.sh/<long random topic>
IGNORE = set(filter(None, os.environ.get("TRIPWIRE_IGNORE", "").split(",")))
QUIET_SECONDS = 300  # one push per source per five minutes
last_alert = {}

HTTP_401 = (b"HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized\r\n"
            b'WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="DS220"\r\n'
            b"Content-Length: 0\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n")


def alert(src, port, body):
    now = time.time()
    if not NTFY or now - last_alert.get(src, 0) < QUIET_SECONDS:
        return
    last_alert[src] = now
    req = urllib.request.Request(NTFY, data=body.encode(), headers={
        "Title": f"tripwire: {src} touched port {port}",
        "Priority": "high",
        "Tags": "rotating_light",
    })
    try:
        urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5)
    except OSError as exc:
        print("ntfy failed:", exc, flush=True)


async def handle(reader, writer, port):
    src = (writer.get_extra_info("peername") or ("?",))[0]
    try:
        if PORTS[port]:
            writer.write(PORTS[port])
            await writer.drain()
        data = await asyncio.wait_for(reader.read(512), timeout=5)
    except (asyncio.TimeoutError, ConnectionError):
        data = b""
    if port == 80 and data:
        writer.write(HTTP_401)
        await writer.drain()
    writer.close()

    # keep the request line, never the Authorization header
    first = data.split(b"\r\n", 1)[0] if port == 80 else data[:120]
    hit = {
        "ts": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
        "src": src,
        "port": port,
        "first_bytes": first.decode("latin-1"),
        "tried_auth": b"Authorization:" in data,
        "ignored": src in IGNORE,
    }
    line = json.dumps(hit)
    with open(LOG, "a") as fh:
        fh.write(line + "\n")
    print(line, flush=True)
    if not hit["ignored"]:
        await asyncio.to_thread(alert, src, port, line)


async def main():
    servers = []
    for port in PORTS:
        servers.append(await asyncio.start_server(
            lambda r, w, p=port: handle(r, w, p), host="0.0.0.0", port=port))
    print("tripwire armed on", ", ".join(map(str, PORTS)), flush=True)
    await asyncio.gather(*(s.serve_forever() for s in servers))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

The SSH port is the quiet star. A real client announces itself before anything else happens, so first_bytes comes back as something like SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.7 or SSH-2.0-libssh2_1.11.0 or a Go library string. That single line tells you whether a person typed ssh or a tool came knocking.

Push alerts go through ntfy, which accepts a plain HTTP POST with Title, Priority and Tags headers. Topics on the public ntfy.sh server work like passwords: anyone who guesses the name can read it. Generate a long one:

$ openssl rand -hex 12

Then subscribe to https://ntfy.sh/ plus that string in the ntfy phone app. If you'd rather keep alerts off someone else's server, ntfy self-hosts in one binary.

Running It Like a Real Service

The tripwire needs ports under 1024, and it should never run as root. systemd handles both: DynamicUser invents a throwaway user, and AmbientCapabilities hands that user exactly one power, binding low ports.

# /etc/systemd/system/tripwire.service
[Unit]
Description=tripwire decoy listeners
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/tripwire/tripwire.py
Environment=TRIPWIRE_NTFY=https://ntfy.sh/9f3c1a7be2d84c06a1b5e7f2
Environment=TRIPWIRE_IGNORE=192.168.1.1
DynamicUser=yes
StateDirectory=tripwire
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Replace the topic with the one you generated. StateDirectory=tripwire gives the dynamic user a writable /var/lib/tripwire, which is where the log lands. Arm it and watch:

$ sudo install -D -m 0755 tripwire.py /opt/tripwire/tripwire.py
$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload
$ sudo systemctl enable --now tripwire
$ journalctl -u tripwire -f

Now trip it yourself, from another machine on the LAN, because you should never trust an alarm you haven't set off:

$ nc -v 192.168.1.50 22
SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13.5
$ curl -i -u admin:admin http://192.168.1.50/
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="DS220"

The log line for that curl shows the request line and "tried_auth": true, with no trace of admin:admin. Your phone should buzz once, then stay quiet for five minutes for that source no matter how hard you hammer it.

The First Week Is Mostly Your Own Junk

Here's where people quit, and where the decoy earns its keep. Arm it and within a day something will hit it, and that something will probably be yours. Windows machines browse for file shares. Network apps like Fing sweep the subnet by design. Home Assistant integrations probe for devices. Some smart TVs knock on everything.

Treat the first week as a census. Count who's touching the box:

$ jq -r '.src' /var/lib/tripwire/hits.jsonl | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

For each address, find the device in your router's client list and decide whether its behavior makes sense. The ones that do go into TRIPWIRE_IGNORE, comma-separated, so they still get logged but stop paging you. The ones you can't explain are the whole reason you built this.

When an alert does point at one of your own machines, say the gaming laptop suddenly sweeping port 445 at 3 AM, the decoy has done its job and the real question moves to that endpoint. What ran, under which parent, using which built-in Windows tool. That's the territory of Living Off the LOLBins ($50), a defensive endpoint guide that maps common signed-tool abuse patterns to the telemetry they should leave behind and shows how to build safe lab scenarios to validate your detections without writing malware. It's the right next read once your tripwire names a machine and you need to know what to look for on it.

Rules of the Trap

Keep this on networks you own or are explicitly allowed to run it on. A decoy in your house is your business. A decoy on your office, dorm or landlord's network is a policy conversation first.

Don't forward these ports to the internet. The public internet scans everything constantly, so an exposed decoy turns into a firehose of meaningless alerts, and you'll mute it within a day. A LAN tripwire stays valuable precisely because its baseline is zero.

Never hack back. The log tells you an address and a fingerprint. What you do next is unplug, investigate your own device, change your own passwords, and call your ISP if it's outside traffic. Touching someone else's machine in return is the line where you stop being the victim.

If you want to go past "something touched it" and actually study what a visitor does after the first knock, which commands get tried, in what order, how they map to known attacker techniques, that belongs in an isolated lab, not on your family network. The Controlled-Lab Honeypot Kit ($65) is built for that step: a decoy controller for a non-production service with no real credentials, visible interaction telemetry, TTP mapping, and a reviewable containment workflow so the experiment never leaks into anything real.

Arm the box tonight, then set it off yourself from the couch. The first real alert is the one you'll be glad you rehearsed.

articles.title: TypeScript Can't Tell userId From orderId. Branded Types Can.
articles.description: TypeScript's structural typing treats userId and orderId as the same type if both are `string` — branded types make them incompatible at compile time.
articles.body_html:
A support engineer is looking at a refund ticket. They copy an ID from one browser tab, paste it into another, and call issueRefund(id). The function signature says id: string. The ID they pasted is a string. TypeScript has nothing to say about it.

The refund goes out. Just not to the customer who filed the ticket — to whoever that ID actually belonged to.

Nobody wrote a bug here. The types were never wrong. That's the part that should bother you.

Two IDs, one type, zero complaints

Here's the function, trimmed to the part that matters:

function issueRefund(userId: string, amountCents: number) {
  // looks up the user, credits their account
}

function getOrder(orderId: string) {
  // fetches the order
}

const order = getOrder("ord_9f21");
issueRefund(order.customerOrderId, 500); // ord_9f21, not a user id

That last line compiles clean. order.customerOrderId is a string. issueRefund wants a string. TypeScript checks shapes, not names — to the compiler, UserId and OrderId were never distinct in the first place, because nobody declared them. They're both just string, and every string is interchangeable with every other string.

This is structural typing, and 95% of the time it's exactly what you want — it's why you can pass a plain object literal anywhere an interface is expected without extending anything. The 5% is IDs, currency amounts, sanitized vs. raw HTML, and anything else where the shape is identical but the meaning isn't allowed to mix.

Spot where you'd make this mistake yourself? Rename the variables and it's not obvious at all — which is exactly why it ships.

Why type UserId = string doesn't help

The first instinct is a type alias:

type UserId = string;
type OrderId = string;

function issueRefund(userId: UserId, amountCents: number) { /* ... */ }

const orderId: OrderId = "ord_9f21";
issueRefund(orderId, 500); // still compiles

Still compiles. A type alias doesn't create a new type — it creates a second name for the same type. UserId and OrderId both resolve to string, so as far as the checker is concerned you wrote issueRefund(id: string, ...) twice. The alias documents intent for a human skimming the code; it does nothing for the compiler.

The fix: give the type something a plain string doesn't have

Branded types close the gap by attaching a marker property that exists only in the type system — never at runtime:

type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly __brand: B };

type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;

function issueRefund(userId: UserId, amountCents: number) { /* ... */ }

function toUserId(raw: string): UserId {
  return raw as UserId;
}

function toOrderId(raw: string): OrderId {
  return raw as OrderId;
}

Now the swap is a compile error:

const orderId = toOrderId("ord_9f21");
issueRefund(orderId, 500);
// Argument of type 'OrderId' is not assignable to parameter of type 'UserId'.
// Type 'OrderId' is not assignable to type '{ readonly __brand: "UserId"; }'.
//   Types of property '__brand' are incompatible.
//     Type '"OrderId"' is not assignable to type '"UserId"'.

UserId and OrderId are both still strings underneath — __brand never appears in a compiled .js file, it's erased along with every other type annotation. It costs nothing at runtime and nothing in bundle size. All it does is give the structural checker something to disagree about, which is the entire point: you're opting one specific type out of structural compatibility.

The only place you're allowed to use as UserId is inside toUserId itself — a narrow, named boundary function. Every other call site just passes a UserId it already has, the same way you'd never cast to string by hand in normal code.

The part branding doesn't do for you

This is the honest caveat, and skipping it is how teams get a false sense of safety: a brand is a label, not a check. toUserId("literally anything") will happily mint a UserId out of a string that was never looked up anywhere. Branding stops a valid OrderId from sneaking into a UserId slot — it does nothing to stop an invalid string from becoming either one.

If you need the value validated too, put a real check inside the boundary function instead of a bare cast:

function toUserId(raw: string): UserId {
  if (!/^usr_[a-z0-9]+$/.test(raw)) {
    throw new Error(`not a valid user id: ${raw}`);
  }
  return raw as UserId;
}

If you're already on a validation library, you likely don't need Brand<> yourself — Zod's .brand() does the same type-level trick and ties it to an actual runtime parse: z.string().brand<"UserId">() gives you a UserId only after the string has actually been validated. Reach for the hand-rolled version above when you're branding something you already trust (a value straight out of your own database row), and a validation library's version when the string is coming from outside — a request body, a query param, a pasted ID in a support ticket.

What you get for it

One type error at the call site instead of a wrong refund in production. No new runtime cost — the brand is erased at compile time like every other TypeScript annotation. No new dependency, if you don't want one. And it generalizes past IDs: money as Brand<number, "Cents"> so you can't add dollars to cents, Brand<string, "SanitizedHtml"> so raw user input can't reach dangerouslySetInnerHTML without passing through your sanitizer first, anywhere "same shape, different meaning" is the actual bug waiting to happen.

The support engineer in the opening scene didn't do anything wrong. The types just never told them userId and orderId were different promises. Now they do.

articles.title: arr[i] Isn't Always There. noUncheckedIndexedAccess Says So.
articles.description: TypeScript types arr[i] as T, never T | undefined — even though the array might be empty. The noUncheckedIndexedAccess flag makes bracket indexing tell the truth.
articles.body_html:
Three lines of TypeScript. Same shape, same compiler, same strict: true.

const user = users.find(u => u.id === id);  // User | undefined
const user2 = userMap.get(id);               // User | undefined
const user3 = usersById[id];                 // User

The first two make you prove the user exists before you touch .name. The third doesn't. It's typed as a plain User — no | undefined, no error, no hint that anything could go wrong. Ship it, and the one time id doesn't match a key, you get Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') in production, from a line TypeScript signed off on.

That's not a fluke in one lib's types. It's the default behavior of [].

The obvious fix that doesn't fix it

Say your team hits this bug, traces it back, and "fixes" the type:

type UsersById = Record<string, User>;
const usersById: UsersById = buildIndex(users);

const user3 = usersById[id];
user3.name; // still typed `User`, still no warning

Nothing changes. Record<string, User> tells TypeScript that every string key maps to a User — which is exactly the lie that caused the bug. An index signature isn't a promise about what's actually in the object; it's a promise about what could be, and TypeScript takes it at face value for every key you ask for, including ones you made up at runtime from user input, a URL param, or a cache miss.

So the team does what teams do under a ticket deadline: they start writing usersById[id]!.name. The ! tells the compiler "trust me, it's there." It compiles. It ships. It's the exact same crash, now with the compiler's blessing instead of its silence.

What's actually going on

arr[i] and obj[key] are indexed access, and TypeScript treats indexed access as a guarantee by default: give it a key of the right type, get back a value of the value type, full stop. It doesn't matter that i could be arr.length or that key could be a string nobody ever inserted — the type signature only describes the shape of a successful lookup, never the possibility of a missing one.

Compare that to Array.prototype.at(), which TypeScript's own lib types declare as at(index: number): T | undefined — not because of any special flag, just because that method's type was written honestly from the start. Or Map.get(), typed V | undefined for the same reason. Those two already tell you the truth. Bracket indexing is the one place TypeScript picked optimism over accuracy, and it's been that way since index signatures existed — strict: true never touched it.

The fix that's actually a compiler flag 

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true
  }
}

Flip this on (it shipped in TypeScript 4.1, and it is not bundled into strict, so turning on strict mode alone will never give you this) and both lines above change shape:

const user3 = usersById[id];        // User | undefined
const n = someArray[i];              // T | undefined
const t: [string, number] = [...];
const first = t[0];                  // still `string` — fixed tuple positions are exempt

Notice what doesn't change: a tuple with a literal, in-bounds index stays exact, because TypeScript can actually verify that position exists at compile time. The flag only widens the cases where it can't — variable array indices and index-signature lookups — which is precisely where the runtime risk lives.

Turning it on is the easy part

The honest downside: flip this in an existing codebase and you'll likely get a wave of new "possibly undefined" errors, all at once, in code that worked yesterday. That's not the flag being noisy. That's every place your code was already one bad lookup away from the same crash, surfacing at once instead of one ticket at a time.

Resist the urge to ! your way through the list. Each one wants a real answer, and the right one depends on where you are in the code:

// You can supply a sane fallback
const label = tags[0] ?? 'untagged';

// You're about to use it repeatedly — narrow once
const user3 = usersById[id];
if (!user3) return notFound();
user3.name; // User, safely

// You actually know more than the type system does
// (a loop invariant, a length check two lines up) — rare, and worth a comment
const first = items[0]!; // items.length checked above

The ! isn't banned — it's just supposed to be the least common answer, reserved for the handful of spots where you can point at why it's safe. If every possibly-undefined error in your list gets the same !, you haven't fixed anything; you've just moved the crash from "silent" to "asserted."

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The one-line trust exercise

noUncheckedIndexedAccess doesn't change a single byte of your compiled JavaScript. The runtime behavior of arr[i] was never in question — it was always capable of returning undefined. All the flag does is make the type checker stop pretending otherwise, for the one kind of access it had been quietly exempting from its own rules.

If your tsconfig.json doesn't have it yet, that's worth fixing before the next usersById[id] ships. What's the last production error you traced back to a lookup TypeScript swore couldn't fail?

articles.title: setCustomValidity() Explained: Native Form Error Messages
articles.description: "Please fill out this field" looks different in every browser and can't be styled or reworded from CSS — so most teams rip out native form validation entirely. setCustomValidity() lets you keep it and still write the message yourself. There's one gotcha that makes it worse than doing nothing if you miss it.
articles.body_html:
Try to submit a signup form with an empty required field in Chrome and you get a little gray bubble: "Please fill out this field." Do the same thing in Firefox and the wording is different. Safari's looks different again. None of the three can be restyled from your CSS, none of them can be translated without translating the browser itself, and none of them match the rest of your form's copy.

So most teams do the obvious thing: add novalidate to the <form>, write their own validation in JavaScript, track an error state per field, wire up aria-live so screen readers hear about it, and manually move focus to the first bad field on submit. It works. It's also several hundred lines reimplementing something the browser was already going to do correctly — for free — if you'd just told it what to say.

The part nobody reaches for: setCustomValidity()

Every form control that participates in constraint validation — <input>, <select>, <textarea>, <button> — has a method called setCustomValidity(message). Call it with a non-empty string, and that string becomes the control's validation message. Everything else about native validation keeps working exactly as before:

const confirmInput = document.querySelector("#confirmPassword");

confirmInput.addEventListener("input", () => {
  if (confirmInput.value !== passwordInput.value) {
    confirmInput.setCustomValidity("Passwords don't match.");
  } else {
    confirmInput.setCustomValidity("");
  }
});

"Passwords match" isn't something type="password" or pattern can express on its own — it's a relationship between two fields, not a shape one field has to match. setCustomValidity() is how you teach the browser's own validation system a rule it doesn't ship with, instead of building a second, parallel validation system next to it.

Call form.reportValidity() on submit (or just let the form submit normally — the browser calls it for you unless novalidate is set), and if confirmPassword has a custom message, the browser focuses that field and shows your text in its native bubble. Screen readers announce it the same way they'd announce "please fill out this field," because as far as the accessibility tree is concerned, nothing about the mechanism changed — only the words did.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The gotcha that makes this worse than doing nothing

Here's where it bites people. setCustomValidity() doesn't expire, doesn't re-check itself, and isn't cleared automatically when the input changes:

// DON'T do this — only ever called once, in the submit handler
form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
  if (confirmInput.value !== passwordInput.value) {
    confirmInput.setCustomValidity("Passwords don't match.");
    e.preventDefault();
  }
  // missing: clearing it back out when the values DO match
});

Set a non-empty custom message once, and confirmInput.validity.valid is false from that point forward — even after the user goes back and fixes the mismatch — because nothing ever told the browser the problem went away. The next submit attempt fails the exact same way, the user retypes an already-correct password over and over, and nobody can tell why. A form that silently refuses to submit is worse than one with no validation at all, because at least "no validation" lets the request through.

The fix is the one line in the first example that's easy to skip: call setCustomValidity("") the moment the condition that caused the error stops being true, every time, not just on submit — typically on every input event, not just on submit. An empty string means "no custom error"; it's not optional cleanup, it's half the API.

checkValidity() vs reportValidity()

Two methods ask "is this valid," and they do different amounts of work:

  • checkValidity() returns true/false and fires an invalid event on any failing control — but shows nothing to the user. Use it when you want the answer without the native UI, e.g. to disable a submit button reactively.
  • reportValidity() does the same check, and if it fails, also shows the browser's validation bubble and moves focus to the first invalid control — the same thing that happens automatically when a form is submitted without novalidate. 
submitButton.disabled = !form.checkValidity(); // silent — just toggles a button
// vs.
saveButton.addEventListener("click", () => form.reportValidity()); // shows the bubble, focuses the field

A button outside the <form> element — in a modal footer, say — can still trigger this with form.requestSubmit(), which runs the same validation reportValidity() would and only proceeds to the submit event if it passes.

Why bother, instead of a validation library

None of this replaces a library for genuinely complex, cross-field, async validation (checking a username against the server, say). What it replaces is the much more common case: a handful of fields where the only problem is that the browser's own wording doesn't match your product's voice, or where one rule — "these two fields must match," "pick at least one checkbox" — doesn't fit a built-in type or pattern. For that case, the browser already has focus management, screen-reader announcement, and :invalid styling working correctly. setCustomValidity() is the one line that lets you keep all of it and just change what it says.

articles.title: Your Framework's Decorators Still Need `experimentalDecorators`
articles.description: TypeScript 5 shipped real, standardized decorators with no flag required — but if your framework injects constructor parameters, deleting experimentalDecorators breaks it, and that's permanent, not a migration lag.
articles.body_html:
You're tidying up tsconfig.json. experimentalDecorators: true has been sitting there since someone copy-pasted it from a tutorial two years ago, and it looks like exactly the kind of thing worth deleting — TypeScript 5 has had real, standardized decorators for a while now, no flag required. You remove the line, save, and run the build.

It goes red in nineteen places. Every one of them is a NestJS service, and every error traces back to a constructor argument.

src/users/users.service.ts:12:30 - error TS1206: Decorators are not valid here.
  constructor(@InjectRepository(User) private repo: Repository<User>) {}
                              ~~~~~~~~

Nothing about that message mentions "legacy" or "standard" decorators. It just says the decorator isn't valid in that position anymore — which is technically true, and tells you nothing about why a flag you just deleted was the thing holding your dependency injection together.

The belief: experimentalDecorators is legacy cruft now

Here's the reasoning, and it's not unreasonable: decorators spent years in TC39 limbo, TypeScript shipped them early and gated them behind experimentalDecorators as a warning label, and in March 2023 TypeScript 5.0 added support for the real, Stage 3 ECMAScript decorators proposal — on by default, no flag at all. "Experimental" sounds temporary. "Standardized" sounds like the upgrade path. Delete the old flag, get the new thing. That's how every other experimentalX flag in tsconfig.json has worked.

Except decorators aren't one feature with two flag states. They're two different features that happen to share a syntax (@something), and only one of the two was ever submitted to TC39.

The crack: parameter decorators don't exist in the new spec

Open the actual TC39 decorators proposal and look at what it lets you attach a decorator to: classes, methods, getters, setters, and fields (including the new accessor keyword for auto-accessors). That's the complete list. Constructor and method parameters aren't in it — not deprioritized, not planned for a later stage, just never part of the proposal TC39 advanced.

That's a problem for a specific, common pattern: frameworks that figure out what to inject by decorating constructor parameters.

// NestJS, Angular, InversifyJS — this exact shape
constructor(
  @Inject(CONFIG_TOKEN) private config: Config,
  private usersService: UsersService,
) {}

@Inject(CONFIG_TOKEN) is a parameter decorator. There is no standard-decorators equivalent — not a different syntax, not a config flag, nothing. The new spec's decorator function signature is (value, context), built for wrapping a class, a method, or a field. A constructor parameter was never something the proposal gave you a way to describe.

So when you turn experimentalDecorators off, TypeScript isn't "modernizing" that decorator. It's telling you the position you put it in no longer accepts one, because under the new rules, it never did.

Why the belief persists

Two things point the same direction and both happen to be wrong.

First, experimentalDecorators sounds provisional by name — and for years it was, in the sense that some decorators feature was always going to graduate out of it eventually. One did. TypeScript's release notes announced "decorators" shipping in 5.0 without the headline distinguishing which half of the old functionality survived the trip through TC39.

Second, most teams meet decorators through a framework, not through the language spec. If you've only ever written @Injectable() and @Inject(), every decorator you've used looks like one feature. There's no moment where the framework tells you "by the way, three of these four decorator kinds have a TC39-standard twin and one doesn't" — you find out when you delete a flag and the build breaks on exactly the one kind that doesn't.

The better mental model: two systems, not one flag

Stop thinking of experimentalDecorators: true → false as a version bump. Treat them as two separate decorator implementations that happen to share an @ symbol:

Legacy (experimentalDecorators: true) Standard (TC39, default since TS 5.0)
Decorator signature (target, propertyKey, descriptor) (value, context)
Can decorate class, method, accessor, property, parameter class, method, getter/setter, field/accessor — no parameters
Metadata emitDecoratorMetadata + reflect-metadata, read via Reflect.getMetadata a separate, still-settling Symbol.metadata proposal — not the same mechanism
Needs a flag? Yes, experimentalDecorators: true No — it's what you get by default

Frameworks whose dependency injection runs through constructor parameters — NestJS and Angular are the two you've most likely used — are built on the legacy system specifically because it's the only one with parameter decorators. That's not these frameworks lagging behind; migrating their DI off constructor parameters would mean redesigning how every existing app wires its services. experimentalDecorators: true in their generated tsconfig.json isn't a leftover setting. It's a requirement with no newer substitute, because the newer spec was never designed to cover this case.

Try the flip side in the playground below: pick "method decorator" instead of "constructor injection," and the exact same toggle that broke the build a second ago compiles clean either way — because a method decorator is one of the cases both systems actually support.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

When turning it off is genuinely fine

This isn't an argument for leaving experimentalDecorators: true everywhere out of caution. If your decorators are method- or class-level — a @Memoize() cache wrapper, a @LogExecutionTime() on a method, MobX's @observable on a field — none of that touches a constructor parameter, and the standard decorators handle it natively. Converting that code is a real decorators 5.0 migration, not an identity crisis, and it drops you to zero legacy flags with nothing structurally in the way.

The test is narrow and mechanical: grep your codebase for a decorator sitting inside a constructor's parameter list. If there's nothing there, flip the flag and watch the build stay green. If there is, that flag isn't debt — it's load-bearing, and it stays until something gives constructor parameters a standard decorator of their own. There's a TC39 proposal for exactly that, Class Method Parameter Decorators — but it's been stuck at Stage 1 since it was last presented in March 2023, so there's no migration path you can actually plan around today.

🧠 Test yourself

Go check your own tsconfig.json. Is experimentalDecorators sitting in there because nobody's gotten around to removing it — or because something in your constructors genuinely needs it? I'd bet a fair number of you find out it's the second one.
